questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q11] In Angular, when using an `AsyncPipe` inside a component template to subscribe to a `BehaviorSubject`, what precise timing mechanism and lifecycle consideration prevents memory leaks and ensures safe cleanup during component destruction?
options: The AsyncPipe utilizes Zone.js microtask queues to hold references; if the BehaviorSubject is not completed manually in ngOnDestroy, the root injector retains the subscription indefinitely.
The AsyncPipe creates an independent internal subscription that persists across component re-creations unless bound using structural directives like *ngIf with safe navigation operators.
The AsyncPipe does not handle unsubscription automatically; instead, it relies on the garbage collector, requiring developers to invoke unsubscribe() in ngOnDestroy to avoid dangling references.

The AsyncPipe automatically subscribes on component initialization and explicitly manages unsubscription when the component instance is destroyed, meaning manual unsubscription is unnecessary for pipes bound in the template.
questions.correctAnswer: The AsyncPipe automatically subscribes on component initialization and explicitly manages unsubscription when the component instance is destroyed, meaning manual unsubscription is unnecessary for pipes bound in the template.
questions.explanation: The AsyncPipe internally subscribes to the Observable during instantiation and automatically unsubscribes when the component or the view containing the binding is destroyed, preventing memory leaks without requiring explicit cleanup code in ngOnDestroy.

questions.relatedConcept: AsyncPipe lifecycle management and automatic unsubscription
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers love asking about subscription management to see if candidates understand how AsyncPipe simplifies memory handling compared to manual subscriptions.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q12] What is the execution order and change detection impact when a Signal is updated inside an Effect within an Angular component that utilizes zoneless change detection (`provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()`)?
options: Angular throws a runtime error preventing infinite loops (e.g., detecting cyclic writes within reactive graph dependencies), because signals cannot be written to synchronously inside an effect computation phase.
The effect executes continuously in a tight synchronous loop until the browser crashes due to a maximum call stack exceeded error.
Zoneless change detection catches the modification, defers the update to the next microtask, and increments the count exactly once without triggering reactive errors.
The effect updates the signal only once because Angular effects are designed with built-in debouncing mechanisms that ignore inner synchronous writes.
questions.correctAnswer: Angular throws a runtime error preventing infinite loops (e.g., detecting cyclic writes within reactive graph dependencies), because signals cannot be written to synchronously inside an effect computation phase.
questions.explanation: Angular's reactive system explicitly disallows writing to signals inside an `effect()` to prevent infinite loops and unpredictable state cycles. Attempting to update a signal synchronously inside its own dependent effect throws a runtime error.

questions.relatedConcept: Angular Signals reactive graph constraints and effect write restrictions
questions.interviewTip: This tests deep knowledge of Angular's new Signals architecture, specifically the guardrails against side-effect cascades and cyclic updates.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q13] When developing an Angular application using Zone.js, what does a persistent 'ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError' during development most fundamentally imply about the component lifecycle?
options: The asynchronous event loop is blocked by an infinite RxJS observable pipe executing continuously in the background.

The Angular compiler detected a circular dependency in the dependency injection container while resolving token metadata.
questions.correctAnswer: A binding or property was mutated during or after the view verification phase, causing a state drift between the model and the DOM before the next change detection cycle began.
questions.explanation: Angular's development-mode change detection runs a secondary verification pass immediately after checking a component tree's views to ensure no bindings changed during the check. If a lifecycle hook (like ngAfterViewChecked) mutates a property bound in the template, the recorded value differs from the newly evaluated value, triggering the ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError.
questions.hint: Think about what phase runs after view rendering and what happens if a component updates its own bound properties during that phase.
questions.relatedConcept: ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError diagnostic analysis in Angular Zone.js lifecycle
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves Angular lifecycle execution order with the internal mechanics of change detection verification passes.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q14] An Angular application exhibits silent subscription leaks and UI components failing to update after router navigation, even though local component variables are assigned correctly inside an injected service. What does this symptom pattern suggest about the service architecture?
options: The service is missing the @Optional decorator, causing the dependency injector to return undefined instances on route changes.
The Observable is cold and multicasted improperly, causing each route navigation to instantiate a fresh execution thread.
The service is provided in 'root' (a singleton), maintaining global state and subscriptions across component destructions without proper unsubscription or lifecycle teardown.
The Ivy renderer has optimized out change detection for services marked with providedIn: 'root'.

questions.explanation: Services provided in 'root' have a singleton lifetime that outlives individual component lifecycles and router navigation events. questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q15] When utilizing `ViewContainerRef.createEmbeddedView()` with a `TemplateRef`, what precise lifecycle and structural mechanics occur regarding custom structural directives and deferred hydration?

It compiles the template string dynamically at runtime into an intermediate Abstract Syntax Tree before appending it to the DOM renderer.

It instantiates the template nodes, attaches the view to the ViewContainerRef tree, inserts the DOM elements immediately into the parent element's location, and runs change detection during the next application tick unless detached.
questions.correctAnswer: It instantiates the template nodes, attaches the view to the ViewContainerRef tree, inserts the DOM elements immediately into the parent element's location, and runs change detection during the next application tick unless detached.
questions.explanation: Calling createEmbeddedView immediately instantiates the template content into DOM nodes, inserts them into the DOM at the ViewContainerRef's relative position, and adds the newly created EmbeddedViewRef to the container's internal view list, participating in subsequent change detection cycles.

questions.relatedConcept: ViewContainerRef and EmbeddedView instantiation lifecycle
questions.interviewTip: Be prepared to explain how dynamic structural directives manipulate host elements and view trees without triggering full component re-bootstrap.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q16] What is the internal execution consequence when an Angular InjectionToken is provided with `providedIn: 'root'` while simultaneously being included in a lazy-loaded feature module's `providers` array?
options: The lazy-loaded module creates a new, isolated injector scope that shadows the root instance, resulting in a distinct service instance being injected into components within that lazy module.

The root-scoped singleton instance is automatically overridden across the entire application, including eagerly loaded components.
Angular merges the provider definitions at compile time, eliminating the duplicate declaration and preserving a single global singleton.
questions.correctAnswer: The lazy-loaded module creates a new, isolated injector scope that shadows the root instance, resulting in a distinct service instance being injected into components within that lazy module.
questions.explanation: Lazy-loaded modules in Angular have their own child injector hierarchy. Providing a token that is already registered with 'root' inside a lazy module's providers array causes the lazy injector to create a new instance local to that lazy module and its children, shadowing the root singleton.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q17] When implementing custom structural directives in Angular using `TemplateRef` and `ViewContainerRef`, what is the primary execution consequence of using `EmbeddedViewRef.destroy()` versus relying solely on `ViewContainerRef.clear()` or structural micro-syntax bindings?
options: Calling `EmbeddedViewRef.destroy()` automatically unlinks the view from the parent `ViewContainerRef` internal indices, mirroring the behavior of `ViewContainerRef.clear()` while freeing memory immediately.

Calling `EmbeddedViewRef.destroy()` permanently detaches and destroys the view, running DOM teardown and triggering associated change detection cleanup, but it leaves the internal tracking pointer inside `ViewContainerRef` stale until explicitly removed from its container index.
Calling `EmbeddedViewRef.destroy()` throws a runtime compilation error because embedded views can only be destroyed via `ViewContainerRef` methods.

Calling `destroy()` on the view ref cleans up the view's bindings, injectors, and DOM nodes, but the parent `ViewContainerRef` may still hold a reference to the destroyed view instance in its internal views collection until explicitly detached or cleared via container methods.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q18] How does Angular's dependency injection system resolve providers when an InjectionToken is provided across multiple hierarchical injector boundaries, specifically when using 'environmentProviders' introduced in Angular 14+ via `makeEnvironmentProviders` versus traditional NgModule providers?
options: Providers created via `makeEnvironmentProviders` (environmentProviders) are strictly restricted to application-root or lazy-loaded route injectors and cannot be overridden by component-level or NgModule-level injectors.

Environment providers (`makeEnvironmentProviders`) restrict provider scope so they cannot be accidentally imported into component `providers` arrays, preventing accidental hierarchical shadowing and mixing of element-level and platform-level dependencies.
Environment providers bypass the hierarchical tree entirely and register directly into the global static root injector regardless of lazy loading boundaries.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q19] When debugging an Angular application using TestBed in a unit test, what is the precise side effect of calling 'TestBed.compileComponents()' asynchronously before creating a component instance?

It builds the production-optimized ahead-of-time (AOT) dependency injection dependency graph for the test suite.
It fetches external HTML and CSS template files via XHR/fetch when component decorators use relative templateUrl or styleUrls paths.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q20] How does Angular's dependency injection hierarchy behave when a service is provided via '@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })' versus being declared in a lazy-loaded feature module's 'providers' array?
options: 'providedIn: 'root'' creates a single application-wide singleton instance, whereas a lazy-loaded module's 'providers' array creates a scoped injector instance unique to that lazy-loaded chunk.

A lazy-loaded module's 'providers' array takes precedence, shadowing the 'root' provider and instantiating a new copy even for eager modules.
'providedIn: 'root'' creates a new singleton per lazy-loaded boundary, while feature module providers are strictly scoped to the root injector.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q21] When leveraging Angular's `bypassSecurityTrustHtml` sanitizer method to render dynamic HTML content, which of the following security implications applies?

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q23] When utilizing Angular's `NgZone.runOutsideAngular` to execute a heavy, third-party non-Angular asynchronous operation, what is the primary architectural implication regarding change detection and UI responsiveness?

Change detection will run twice as fast because the framework prioritizes tasks executed in the outer zone.
Callbacks executed inside the callback block will bypass the Angular zone entirely, preventing microtasks and macrotasks from triggering automatic View/Component dirty-checking cycles.
questions.correctAnswer: Callbacks executed inside the callback block will bypass the Angular zone entirely, preventing microtasks and macrotasks from triggering automatic View/Component dirty-checking cycles.
questions.explanation: Executing code via `runOutsideAngular` detaches the execution context from Angular's custom Zone (`NgZone`). As a result, any asynchronous events (like `setInterval` or DOM events) triggered within that block will not automatically invoke `ApplicationRef.tick()`, saving significant CPU cycles from redundant change detection runs. To update the view, developers must explicitly call `ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges()` or re-enter the zone.
questions.hint: Think about how Angular knows when to trigger change detection and what happens when an event escapes its wrapped zone.
questions.relatedConcept: NgZone and Performance Optimization
questions.interviewTip: Senior interviewers look for deep understanding of Angular's change detection triggers and how to optimize high-frequency event streams (like mousemove or scroll) using NgZone.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q24] What is the primary architectural difference between an Angular Route Resolver and utilizing `async` pipe inside a component template for data fetching during navigation?
options: Route Resolvers block navigation completion until the observable emits and completes, whereas `async` pipe renders the component immediately and resolves data asynchronously within the template lifecycle.
Route Resolvers automatically cache HTTP requests globally, while `async` pipe forces a fresh server fetch on every template render.
Route Resolvers are exclusively designed for standalone components, whereas `async` pipe only works in NgModule-based applications.
Using an `async` pipe prevents the router from throwing navigation cancellation errors if an HTTP request fails.
questions.correctAnswer: Route Resolvers block navigation completion until the observable emits and completes, whereas `async` pipe renders the component immediately and resolves data asynchronously within the template lifecycle.
questions.explanation: A Route Resolver runs prior to route activation, delaying the navigation transition until the resolved data is fully available. Conversely, using an `async` pipe lets the component render immediately in a loading state, fetching and rendering the data asynchronously as the observable emits.
questions.hint: Consider the user experience and navigation lifecycle when a slow network request is tied to a route change versus an in-component subscription.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Routers, Resolvers, and Reactive Data Fetching
questions.interviewTip: Interfering with navigation via resolvers can cause perceived performance bottlenecks if not handled properly. Discussing when to use resolvers versus component-level fetching is a hallmark of a senior frontend engineer.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q25] In Angular, when using the `inject()` function outside of an injection context (such as inside a standard asynchronous callback or a custom class method invoked after component initialization), what behavior occurs?
options: It successfully resolves and returns the dependency by capturing the lexical scope of the component instance at compile time.
It throws a RuntimeError because the reactive injection context has been lost outside the synchronous execution of an injection factory or constructor/field initializer.
It returns undefined and logs a warning to the console, allowing graceful degradation of the service lookup.
It falls back to the root injector context automatically, ignoring component-level providers.
questions.correctAnswer: It throws a RuntimeError because the reactive injection context has been lost outside the synchronous execution of an injection factory or constructor/field initializer.
questions.explanation: The `inject()` function relies on a globally maintained tracking mechanism during the execution phase of injection contexts (such as constructor, field initializers, and factory functions). Once control flow leaves the synchronous execution stack (like inside a `setTimeout` callback or an async/await boundary), the active injector context is cleared, causing `inject()` to throw an error.
questions.hint: Think about when the injection context is active during a component's lifecycle and event loop turns.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Dependency Injection Context and inject() mechanics
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify whether the candidate understands the underlying mechanics of modern Angular's `inject()` function versus traditional constructor injection.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q26] What is the primary architectural reason that Angular signals are designed with synchronous pull-based evaluation instead of automatic push-based reactive streams (like RxJS BehaviorSubjects)?
options: To enforce that all state changes must happen exclusively inside Angular Zone.js interception blocks to trigger change detection.
To bypass TypeScript's type checking system for deeply nested reactive data structures.
To guarantee glitch-free execution where derived computations (computed) are evaluated lazily only when read, eliminating redundant intermediate recalculations in diamond dependency graphs.
To allow native browser garbage collection to immediately reclaim memoized values on every read operation.
questions.correctAnswer: To guarantee glitch-free execution where derived computations (computed) are evaluated lazily only when read, eliminating redundant intermediate recalculations in diamond dependency graphs.
questions.explanation: Signals use a pull-based, lazy evaluation model combined with a push notification of dirty state. When a dependency changes, dependents are only marked as dirty. They are not recalculated until explicitly read (pulled). This prevents the 'glitch' problem common in naive push architectures where intermediate values in a diamond dependency graph might be evaluated multiple times.
questions.hint: Consider how computed values decide when to recalculate relative to when they are accessed.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Signals pull-based reactivity and glitch-free evaluation
questions.interviewTip: Crucial question for senior roles to distinguish between RxJS push-based streams and fine-grained signal reactivity.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q27] When using Angular's 'APP_INITIALIZER' injection token to run asynchronous startup tasks before the application completely bootstraps, what happens if one of the provider factories returns an observable that completes without emitting any value?
options: The application bootstrap fails because APP_INITIALIZER expects at least one emitted value from the observable.
Angular ignores the observable entirely and throws a runtime NullInjectorError.
The application enters an infinite bootstrap loading state waiting for a emission.
Angular waits for the observable to complete and successfully proceeds with application bootstrapping.
questions.correctAnswer: Angular waits for the observable to complete and successfully proceeds with application bootstrapping.
questions.explanation: Angular's APP_INITIALIZER relies on 'toPromise()' or firstValueFrom-like resolution under the hood which resolves upon completion of the returned Promise/Observable. Emitting a value is not strictly required as long as the observable successfully completes.
questions.hint: Consider whether completion alone is sufficient or if an emission is mandatory for stream resolution.
questions.relatedConcept: APP_INITIALIZER stream completion semantics
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of RxJS stream lifecycles in conjunction with Angular's core platform initialization tokens.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q28] In an Angular application utilizing Zone.js, what is the precise side-effect of executing an asynchronous task inside a function wrapped with 'NgZone.runOutsideAngular' when that task eventually mutates a component property bound in the template?
options: The component property updates in memory, but the view does not reflect the change immediately because no change detection cycle is scheduled by Zone.js.
The component property updates immediately, and Angular automatically triggers a change detection cycle because Zone.js intercepts all timers.
Angular throws a NgZoneOptimizedExecutionError preventing mutations outside the zone.
The application crashes due to a cross-zone thread synchronization violation.
questions.correctAnswer: The component property updates in memory, but the view does not reflect the change immediately because no change detection cycle is scheduled by Zone.js.
questions.explanation: When code runs outside the Angular zone, asynchronous callbacks like setTimeout do not trigger Angular's automatic change detection mechanism. The model updates, but the DOM view remains stale until another event forces change detection.
questions.hint: Think about what Zone.js listens to in order to trigger automatic change detection cycles.
questions.relatedConcept: NgZone runOutsideAngular change detection implication
questions.interviewTip: Crucial for performance tuning discussions where developers optimize high-frequency events (like mousemoves) by bypassing change detection.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q29] When leveraging Angular's `NgZone.runOutsideAngular` to execute high-frequency DOM event handlers or third-party animations, what is the precise performance implication on change detection cycles?
options: It completely disables Zone.js globally across the entire application instance for the lifetime of the component.
It prevents Zone.js from intercepting the macro/microtasks inside the callback, halting automatic dirty-checking propagation for that event stream until manually re-entered or triggered.
It converts synchronous event emissions into asynchronous Promises, delaying execution until the next microtask queue flush.
It forces the component to permanently switch to OnPush change detection strategy, ignoring all subsequent @Input changes.
questions.correctAnswer: It prevents Zone.js from intercepting the macro/microtasks inside the callback, halting automatic dirty-checking propagation for that event stream until manually re-entered or triggered.
questions.explanation: Executing code via `runOutsideAngular` detaches the specified execution context from Zone.js interception. Consequently, asynchronous operations or events triggered within this block do not automatically notify Angular to run a global change detection pass, drastically reducing CPU overhead during high-frequency events.
questions.hint: Consider how Zone.js hooks into asynchronous operations and how Angular's tick() gets triggered.
questions.relatedConcept: NgZone optimization and change detection mitigation
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to test whether candidates understand how Angular bridges underlying browser events to framework-level change detection via Zone.js.

questions.question: [Angular • Test 1 • Q30] In an Angular application utilizing `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`, under which specific condition will a component NOT re-render even when a local service injected into it updates its internal RxJS BehaviorSubject state?
options: It will always re-render automatically because BehaviorSubject triggers an immediate change detection cycle upon emission.
It will fail to re-render if the service method is invoked from outside the Angular zone.
If the template does NOT use the async pipe, or if the service instance is scoped locally via component providers rather than 'root'.
It will not re-render if the component has child components using Default change detection.
questions.correctAnswer: If the template does NOT use the async pipe, or if the service instance is scoped locally via component providers rather than 'root'.
questions.explanation: With `OnPush`, Angular only checks a component if an `@Input` reference changes, an event originates from the component/children, or an async pipe receives a new emission. If the service is injected and state is mutated/emitted without an async pipe binding in the template or an explicit `markForCheck()` call, OnPush prevents the view from updating.
questions.hint: Remember that OnPush components are immune to service state mutations unless explicitly flagged or bound via specific pipes.
questions.relatedConcept: OnPush change detection and reactive state binding mechanisms
questions.interviewTip: This tests the boundary between RxJS observables and Angular's rendering lifecycle optimization under OnPush.

title: Vue - Test 1: Core Fundamentals & Patterns
description: Comprehensive technical evaluation for Vue covering runtime mechanics, design principles, and problem solving.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q1] What happens when you declare a ref inside a Vue 3 computed property callback function?
options: Vue throws a runtime error because refs cannot be initialized inside computed properties.
A new reactive ref is instantiated on every computation run, leading to memory overhead and broken reactive dependency tracking across updates.
The inner ref is cached after the first execution and behaves identically to a normal variable.
The ref is hoisted to the component scope automatically during the compilation phase.
questions.correctAnswer: A new reactive ref is instantiated on every computation run, leading to memory overhead and broken reactive dependency tracking across updates.
questions.explanation: Declaring a ref inside a computed getter causes it to re-initialize every time the computed property evaluates. This not only wastes memory but creates a fresh, untracked reactive reference on each run, which breaks expected component state flow and violates reactivity rules.
questions.hint: Consider where reactive primitives should be instantiated relative to evaluation cycles.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Composition API Ref Lifecycle
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if a candidate truly understands Vue's reactivity initialization lifecycle versus side-effect-free pure getters.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q2] In Vue 3, what is the precise runtime behavior of unwrapping a reactive object that contains nested plain objects or refs when passed to `toRefs`?
options: toRefs recursively converts all nested properties at any depth into individual refs.
toRefs throws a TypeError because nested objects are not natively supported.
toRefs only flattens the top-level properties of the reactive object; nested objects remain plain objects and their properties do not become individual refs.
nested becomes a computed ref that evaluates lazily.
questions.correctAnswer: toRefs only flattens the top-level properties of the reactive object; nested objects remain plain objects and their properties do not become individual refs.
questions.explanation: vue's `toRefs` is shallow by design. It only creates refs for the top-level properties of the reactive object passed to it. Deep conversion requires manual nested calls or specialized helper utilities.
questions.hint: Check whether toRefs operates recursively or shallowly on properties.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 toRefs Shallow Conversion
questions.interviewTip: Useful for verifying deep understanding of reactivity unwrapping limitations when destructuring state.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q3] What happens when you declare a Vue 3 computed property that modifies its own source reactive dependency during evaluation?
options: The computed property caches the value normally without side effects
The source property remains unchanged because computed properties are strictly read-only proxies
Vue automatically defers the mutation to the next tick without issue
Vue throws a runtime warning or triggers an infinite recursive update loop
questions.correctAnswer: Vue throws a runtime warning or triggers an infinite recursive update loop
questions.explanation: Computed properties are intended to be pure functions that only evaluate and return derived state. Mutating reactive state inside a computed getter triggers side effects during the render or dependency-tracking phase, leading to infinite trigger loops or warnings.
questions.hint: Think about purity vs side effects in reactivity getters.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Computed Property Purity and Side Effects
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates understand reactive lifecycle rules and functional purity in computed getters.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q4] In Vue 3, what occurs if you destructure reactive properties directly from a reactive object returned by 'reactive()' and pass them into child components?
options: The properties lose their reactivity connection, becoming plain primitive values in the template
The properties automatically become independent ref objects
Vue throws a compile-time SyntaxError
Reactivity is fully preserved via proxy prototype delegation
questions.correctAnswer: The properties lose their reactivity connection, becoming plain primitive values in the template
questions.explanation: ES6 destructuring copies the values at the time of destructuring. Because they are copied as primitive values, they lose the reactive proxy connection, requiring 'toRefs()' to maintain reactivity when destructuring.
questions.hint: Remember how ES6 destructuring handles JavaScript primitive references versus reactive proxies.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Reactive Destructuring Pitfall
questions.interviewTip: This is a classic trap when transitioning from Options API to Composition API, frequently asked to test reactivity mechanics.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q5] When utilizing functional components in Vue 3 with compiler hints, what is the primary architectural trade-off regarding performance and reactivity?
questions.codeSnippet: const CustomBtn = (props, { slots }) => h('button', props, slots.default())
options: Functional components render significantly slower than stateful components because they execute the template compilation pipeline on every single mount.
Functional components lack stateful instance creation overhead, but skip internal lifecycle hooks and automated proxy reactivity tracking for local properties.
Functional components automatically memoize all computed properties, causing high memory consumption in large dynamic tables.
Functional components require a complete Virtual DOM reconciliation bail-out, turning off patch optimization flags entirely.
questions.correctAnswer: Functional components lack stateful instance creation overhead, but skip internal lifecycle hooks and automated proxy reactivity tracking for local properties.
questions.explanation: Functional components in Vue 3 are stateless and instanceless, rendering extremely fast with low memory overhead because they bypass reactive proxy wrapping and lifecycle hook management. The trade-off is the loss of internal state and standard instance APIs.
questions.hint: Consider the lack of a backing stateful instance (no 'this' or reactive state proxy).
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Functional Component Architecture & Performance
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask about functional components to check your understanding of memory overhead versus feature sets in high-frequency rendering scenarios like data grids.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q6] What is the underlying rendering mechanism trade-off when using `v-memo` on a large list item v-for loop in Vue 3?
questions.codeSnippet: <div v-for="item in list" :key="item.id" v-memo="[item.version]">...
options: It forces the component to compile into a static render function, preventing any dynamic CSS bindings inside the loop.
It completely disables key-based reconciliation, relying exclusively on index-based array splicing during updates.

It caches the entire VNode tree and completely bypasses both template parsing and shallow reactivity checks if dependency arrays remain unchanged, trading minor memory usage for massive diffing speedups.
It moves the element evaluation into a Web Worker, eliminating UI thread blocking during layout shifts.
questions.correctAnswer: It caches the entire VNode tree and completely bypasses both template parsing and shallow reactivity checks if dependency arrays remain unchanged, trading minor memory usage for massive diffing speedups.
questions.explanation: v-memo allows Vue to skip VNode creation and diffing for sub-trees when the specified dependency array hasn't changed. This trades a small amount of memory overhead to cache dependency arrays for massive optimization on large lists.
questions.hint: Think about conditional caching of VNode sub-trees based on dependency arrays.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 v-memo Performance Optimization and Sub-tree Caching
questions.interviewTip: Senior candidates should be able to explain when to apply v-memo versus when it becomes premature optimization due to the overhead of array comparisons.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q7] In Vue 3, why is mutating a reactive object property passed down from a parent component via a direct prop reference generally flagged as an anti-pattern by code reviewers?
options: It causes an immediate runtime TypeError because props are frozen withObject.freeze() internally in Vue 3.
It completely disables the Vue template reactivity wrapper, rendering the property immutable for all subsequent renders.
It triggers an infinite component re-rendering loop by automatically emitting an unhandled 'update:modelValue' event.
It violates unidirectional data flow, making state mutations untraceable and prone to parent-child synchronization conflicts.
questions.correctAnswer: It violates unidirectional data flow, making state mutations untraceable and prone to parent-child synchronization conflicts.
questions.explanation: While JavaScript objects passed as props are passed by reference and mutating their nested properties won't throw a direct error, doing so bypasses Vue's unidirectional data flow model. This breaks debugging guarantees because state changes originate inside a child component rather than the owner, obscuring the source of truth.
questions.hint: Think about how data flow ownership and debugging are impacted when children modify parent-owned references directly.
questions.relatedConcept: Unidirectional data flow and prop mutation antipatterns in Vue 3
questions.interviewTip: Intermediary to senior interviewers love asking this to see if candidates understand the distinction between structural JS pass-by-reference behavior and Vue's architectural data-flow principles.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q8] What is the primary architectural pitfall of placing asynchronous API calls directly inside a Vue computed property getter?
options: Computed properties expect synchronous return values to track dependencies correctly; asynchronous promises cause them to evaluate to a Promise object rather than the resolved data, breaking templates.
Computed properties automatically throw a compilation error if an 'async' keyword or 'await' operator is detected inside their getter function.
Async operations inside computed properties bypass Vue's virtual DOM diffing algorithm entirely, causing memory leaks.
It causes the Vue compiler to treat the computed property as a static constant, preventing any future invalidation.
questions.correctAnswer: Computed properties expect synchronous return values to track dependencies correctly; asynchronous promises cause them to evaluate to a Promise object rather than the resolved data, breaking templates.
questions.explanation: Computed properties are designed to be synchronous, side-effect-free calculations derived from reactive state. If an async function is used, the computed property returns a Promise object immediately instead of the resolved value, and Vue cannot track asynchronous dependencies inside the getter. Side effects and async requests belong in watchers or lifecycle hooks.
questions.hint: Consider what a computed getter actually returns when marked as 'async' and how templates consume that return value.
questions.relatedConcept: Computed property side-effect constraints and async limitations
questions.interviewTip: Reviewers frequently look out for this when developers try to treat computed properties like useEffect or data-fetching hooks.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q9] In Vue 3, when employing a `v-for` directive over a dynamic array where items are frequently reordered, what is the precise impact of omitting the `key` attribute on component instance preservation and DOM recycling?
options: Vue completely re-creates the entire list parent container on every mutation, triggering a full unmount and remount cycle for all child nodes.
Vue falls back to an 'in-place patch' index-based strategy, which can cause state corruption or incorrect data rendering if child components maintain local state.
Vue throws a runtime warning in development mode and automatically assigns a cryptographic hash to each DOM node as a pseudo-key.
Vue optimizes rendering by treating the list as an immutable static tree, entirely skipping reactivity tracking for elements inside the loop.
questions.correctAnswer: Vue falls back to an 'in-place patch' index-based strategy, which can cause state corruption or incorrect data rendering if child components maintain local state.
questions.explanation: By default, Vue uses an 'in-place patch' strategy. If the order of data items changes, instead of moving the DOM elements to match the order, Vue patches each element in-place to ensure it reflects what should be at that index. This causes issues if the DOM node relies on transient local state or sub-component state keyed to specific data items.
questions.hint: Think about how Vue matches old and new VNodes when no explicit identifier is provided.
questions.relatedConcept: v-for key attribute and reconciliation algorithm
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers often ask this to check if candidates understand virtual DOM diffing mechanics and state preservation pitfalls in lists.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q10] What is the primary memory and lifecycle implication of failing to unregister a global event listener inside a Vue component's `onUnmounted` lifecycle hook (Composition API)?
options: Vue's compiler automatically detects un-cleaned global listeners during teardown and strips them at compile-time.
The event handler continues to fire harmlessly, but the memory allocated for the listener is garbage collected as soon as the DOM nodes are detached.
It results in a memory leak because the component instance closure and its associated reactive references remain retained in memory via the global event handler reference.
It causes a fatal navigation crash due to conflicting event execution contexts between separate view states.
questions.correctAnswer: It results in a memory leak because the component instance closure and its associated reactive references remain retained in memory via the global event handler reference.
questions.explanation: Global event targets like `window` or `document` retain a strong reference to the callback function passed to `addEventListener`. If the component instance is unmounted without calling `removeEventListener`, the callback—and by closure scope, the component instance and its reactive scope—cannot be garbage collected, resulting in a memory leak.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to closures when an external object holds a reference to a function defined inside a component setup scope.
questions.relatedConcept: Component lifecycle cleanup and memory leaks
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to evaluate practical production awareness regarding memory management and cleanup habits in single-page applications.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q11] In Vue 3 Composition API, when should side effects that mutate DOM elements or perform asynchronous data fetching be executed relative to the component lifecycle?
options: Directly inside the setup() function body during synchronous execution to ensure immediate setup
Inside computed properties to leverage memoization for performance optimization
Inside template expressions to keep data binding declarative and side-effect free
Inside onMounted or watcher callbacks to guarantee the reactive scope and DOM nodes are fully initialized
questions.correctAnswer: Inside onMounted or watcher callbacks to guarantee the reactive scope and DOM nodes are fully initialized
questions.explanation: In Vue 3, setup() executes before the component is mounted to the DOM. Executing DOM mutations or async fetching directly in setup() lacks access to rendered DOM elements and can cause SSR hydration mismatches. Using lifecycle hooks like onMounted ensures proper DOM availability.
questions.hint: Think about when the actual DOM nodes are created and attached in a component's lifecycle.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 setup lifecycle and side effect management
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers check this to see if candidates understand Vue's reactivity initialization vs. DOM-dependent side effects.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q12] How does Vue 3 handle state updates when multiple reactive properties are mutated synchronously within a custom asynchronous event handler or macro task?
options: All mutations are batched into a single microtask queue and flushed asynchronously before the next browser paint
Each individual property mutation triggers an immediate, synchronous DOM re-render
Vue blocks the JavaScript main thread until all component sub-trees are fully synchronized
Mutations inside async tasks are ignored unless wrapped explicitly in $forceUpdate()
questions.correctAnswer: All mutations are batched into a single microtask queue and flushed asynchronously before the next browser paint
questions.explanation: Vue queues state mutations and buffers them in a queue to avoid redundant DOM re-renders when multiple state variables change within the same tick. The batching is flushed asynchronously via microtasks (like Promise.resolve() or MutationObserver).
questions.hint: Consider how Vue optimizes multiple synchronous state changes before updating the DOM.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue asynchronous rendering queue and DOM batching
questions.interviewTip: This tests deep knowledge of Vue's internal scheduler and asynchronous update cycle performance optimizations.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q13] When developing a Vue 3 application using the Composition API, you notice that mutating a property of a reactive object inside a nested child component does not trigger the expected UI update in a parent component computed property. Which of the following root causes best explains this symptom?
options: Provide/inject injections are read-only by default and silently block mutation attempts across component boundaries.
Destructuring reactive objects strips away their proxy reactivity wrappers, decoupling the local variable from the reactive source.
Nested objects inside reactive() calls automatically convert to shallowReactive, requiring manual deep tracking.
Computed properties cannot depend on values injected from a parent component unless explicitly wrapped in a watchEffect.
questions.correctAnswer: Destructuring reactive objects strips away their proxy reactivity wrappers, decoupling the local variable from the reactive source.
questions.explanation: Destructuring a reactive object created via reactive() breaks the reactivity connection because primitive values obtained via destructuring are plain values, not getter/setter proxies. The mutation or usage of the destructured variable will not track dependencies.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to JavaScript references when you destructure properties from a reactive proxy.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 reactive destructuring caveat and proxy loss
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates understand the limitations of JavaScript proxies when dealing with destructuring in Vue 3.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q14] In a Vue 3 application, a component's lifecycle hook `onMounted` fires, but attempts to query or manipulate a DOM element via a template ref yield `null`. Which of the following code patterns typically causes this specific symptom?
options: Template refs in Vue 3 cannot be accessed inside `onMounted` and must be delayed using `nextTick` unconditionally.
The `ref` variable name does not match the string attribute name provided in the template.
The element is conditionally rendered via `v-if`, and its initial evaluation evaluates to false during the mount phase.
Script setup syntax scopes template refs locally, preventing them from being exposed to lifecycle hooks.
questions.correctAnswer: The element is conditionally rendered via `v-if`, and its initial evaluation evaluates to false during the mount phase.
questions.explanation: If an element has a `v-if` directive that evaluates to false when the component mounts, it does not exist in the DOM, resulting in the template ref remaining `null` even inside `onMounted`.
questions.hint: Check conditional rendering directives attached to the element carrying the template ref.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue template refs with conditional rendering (v-if)
questions.interviewTip: This tests practical debugging skills regarding conditional rendering interactions with template refs in Vue.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q15] What happens when you pass a reactive object returned by `reactive()` directly into a Vue 3 `provide` call and consume it using `inject()` in a deeply nested descendant component?
options: The injected object loses reactivity because provide/inject strips Proxies during the context transfer.
Vue throws a runtime warning because reactive objects cannot be passed down via provide/inject without being wrapped in a computed property.
Mutations throw a readonly error unless the injected object is explicitly declared inside a readonly wrapper.
The injected object remains fully reactive, and mutations to its properties trigger updates across all consuming components.
questions.correctAnswer: The injected object remains fully reactive, and mutations to its properties trigger updates across all consuming components.
questions.explanation: In Vue 3, objects wrapped in `reactive()` maintain their Proxy-based reactivity when passed via `provide` and consumed via `inject`. Mutations made on the injected reference in descendant components will properly trigger reactivity updates.
questions.hint: Consider whether Vue's Proxy wrappers are preserved across the dependency injection context boundary.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Composition API Provide/Inject Reactivity Preservation
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to test your understanding of how Vue 3 maintains state synchronization and reactivity across component tree boundaries via provide and inject.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q16] In Vue 3, what is the precise behavior of the `v-memo` directive when its dependency array is passed as an empty array `v-memo="[]"`?
questions.codeSnippet: {{ expensiveComputation }}
options: The template block is cached permanently after the initial render and will never update, even if component-level reactive dependencies change.
The template block re-evaluates and updates on every single component re-render cycle, effectively disabling optimization.
Vue throws a compilation error because `v-memo` requires at least one dependency expression inside its array.
The block behaves identically to `v-once`, but only caches internal child components rather than DOM nodes.
questions.correctAnswer: The template block is cached permanently after the initial render and will never update, even if component-level reactive dependencies change.
questions.explanation: When an empty array `[]` is passed to `v-memo`, the memoized template block will never re-evaluate or update after its initial render, since none of its dependencies ever change. This is functionally similar to `v-once` but scoped to a specific DOM subtree.
questions.hint: Think about what an empty dependency array means for conditional re-evaluation triggers in memoization algorithms.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 v-memo Directive Optimization Behavior
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify whether candidates know advanced performance optimization techniques beyond standard computed properties and lazy loading.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q17] In Vue 3, how does the behavior of `v-model` change when applied to a custom component compared to Vue 2?
questions.codeSnippet: <MyComponent v-model:title="pageTitle" />
options: Vue 3 automatically infers the prop name from the component's internal name attribute rather than requiring explicit prop definitions.
Vue 3 replaces the default 'value' prop and 'input' event with 'modelValue' prop and 'update:modelValue' event, while supporting named model arguments.
Vue 3 removes custom component v-model support entirely, forcing developers to use explicit property bindings and custom event emitters.
Vue 3 retains the exact same 'value' prop and 'input' event contract from Vue 2, but wraps them in a Proxy for reactivity.
questions.correctAnswer: Vue 3 replaces the default 'value' prop and 'input' event with 'modelValue' prop and 'update:modelValue' event, while supporting named model arguments.
questions.explanation: Vue 3 standardizes `v-model` on custom components to use `modelValue` as the prop and `update:modelValue` as the emitted event by default, and introduces argument syntax like `v-model:title` to support multiple bindings on a single component.
questions.hint: Think about what props and events are automatically generated by the compiler for v-model in Vue 3.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Custom Component v-model API Changes
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers often ask this to verify migration knowledge from Vue 2 to Vue 3 and understanding of template compilation semantics.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q18] What is the primary architectural difference in how Vue 3 handles multiple root nodes in a Single File Component (SFC) template compared to Vue 2?
questions.codeSnippet:
<template>
  <header>Header</header>
  <main>Content</main>
</template>
options: Vue 3 automatically injects a hidden <div> wrapper around multiple roots during compilation to satisfy DOM tree requirements.
Vue 3 throws a compilation error unless a single functional wrapper or <template v-slot> is provided.
Vue 3 supports Fragments out of the box, allowing components to have multiple root nodes without a wrapper element by explicitly patching the VNode children array.
Vue 3 delegates multiple root management entirely to the browser's native Shadow DOM implementation.
questions.correctAnswer: Vue 3 supports Fragments out of the box, allowing components to have multiple root nodes without a wrapper element by explicitly patching the VNode children array.
questions.explanation: Unlike Vue 2 which strictly enforced a single root element per SFC template, Vue 3 introduces Fragment support natively, allowing a component to render multiple root nodes and intelligently managing them via a flat VNode children array structure.
questions.hint: Consider the concept of 'Fragments' introduced in modern frontend frameworks to avoid unnecessary wrapper DOM nodes.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Template Fragments and Multi-Root Architecture
questions.interviewTip: This question tests understanding of virtual DOM improvements and DOM structure optimization in Vue 3.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q19] When testing a Vue 3 component that uses Pinia stores via Vitest, what is the primary consequence of failing to call `setActivePinia()` before mounting the component with `mount()`?
options: The component will mount successfully, but all reactive store properties will remain permanently undefined.
Vue Test Utils will automatically create a fallback global Pinia store with default initial state values.
Vitest will intercept the missing store call and return mocked data using automatic file-system mocks.
Pinia will throw an active pinia was not found error because no store instance can be located or initialized.
questions.correctAnswer: Pinia will throw an active pinia was not found error because no store instance can be located or initialized.
questions.explanation: Pinia relies on an active instance of the pinia plugin to bind stores to the current Vue application context. Without `setActivePinia()` or passing a pinia instance directly to the test mount options (`global: { plugins: [pinia] }`), any attempt to use a store inside the component throws a runtime error stating that an active Pinia was not found.
questions.hint: Think about how Pinia tracks the current application context during unit testing outside of `app.use(pinia)`.
questions.relatedConcept: Pinia testing context and setActivePinia in Vue 3
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to verify practical experience with Vue 3 state management unit testing pitfalls and error diagnostics.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q20] How does Vue's Reactivity Transform (deprecated/experimental macro approach) or compiler-hinted error tracking behave when unref() is omitted in a custom Vue composition function diagnostic logger?
options: watchEffect tracks the ref object container itself rather than its .value property, causing the effect not to trigger on value mutations unless .value is accessed.
Vue's compiler automatically unwraps all arguments passed to custom functions inside watchEffect blocks.
Passing a ref directly to console.log throws a TypeError because refs cannot be read inside synchronous effects.
The effect executes once on mount and permanently unregisters itself due to type mismatch.
questions.correctAnswer: watchEffect tracks the ref object container itself rather than its .value property, causing the effect not to trigger on value mutations unless .value is accessed.
questions.explanation: Reactivity in Vue is tracked when `.value` is read, which triggers dependency collection (track). If you pass a `Ref` object directly into a logging function or watch effect without reading its `.value` property, the tracking mechanism binds to the `.value` property slot only if accessed, or fails to track property mutations accurately if the ref wrapper itself is monitored rather than its inner primitive value.
questions.hint: Consider how Vue's dependency tracking hooks into property and value accessors.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue reactivity dependency tracking and ref unwrapping pitfalls
questions.interviewTip: Used to test deep comprehension of Vue's Proxy-based reactivity tracking internals and debugging side effects.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q21] When utilizing the `v-html` directive in Vue to render untrusted user-supplied content, what is the primary security vulnerability introduced, and how does Vue's architecture handle it?
options: It triggers a hydration mismatch error during Server-Side Rendering (SSR) but is automatically sanitized by the Vue template compiler against XSS.
It introduces a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability because Vue does not sanitize HTML strings bound via v-html before inserting them into the DOM.
It automatically escapes script tags and malicious event handlers, protecting against XSS while allowing basic formatting.
It violates Content Security Policy (CSP) headers exclusively in production builds, disabling template compilation entirely.
questions.correctAnswer: It introduces a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability because Vue does not sanitize HTML strings bound via v-html before inserting them into the DOM.
questions.explanation: Dynamically rendering arbitrary HTML on your website can easily lead to XSS vulnerabilities because it's very easy for malicious third parties to inject arbitrary JavaScript execution vectors. Vue's `v-html` explicitly bypasses Vue's standard text interpolation (which automatically escapes content) and inserts raw HTML directly into the DOM.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to raw HTML strings when passed to innerHTML in a browser environment.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue v-html directive and Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) risks
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to test whether developers understand the security implications of bypassing Vue's template sanitization safeguards.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q22] What is the primary security risk of passing raw, untrusted user input directly into Vue's dynamic component or asynchronous component definitions (e.g., `:is='userInput'`), and how can it be mitigated?
questions.codeSnippet: <component :is="userInputControl"></component>
options: It causes a memory leak because dynamic components are never garbage collected by Vue's reactivity system.
It leads to a prototype pollution vulnerability inside the Vue virtual DOM diffing algorithm.
It allows an attacker to instantiate arbitrary registered components, potentially exposing internal admin modules or triggering unwanted lifecycle side-effects if unvalidated.
It throws a compilation syntax error because dynamic component bindings only accept string literal identifiers, not variables.
questions.correctAnswer: It allows an attacker to instantiate arbitrary registered components, potentially exposing internal admin modules or triggering unwanted lifecycle side-effects if unvalidated.
questions.explanation: If a dynamic component's identifier (`:is`) is driven by unsanitized user input or unvalidated route parameters, an attacker might supply names of internal, sensitive, or unintended components registered globally or locally, leading to unauthorized UI exposure or logic execution.
questions.hint: Consider what `:is` resolves against in the component registry.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue dynamic components and security boundary enforcement
questions.interviewTip: This tests advanced awareness of component registry hijacking and input validation boundaries in Vue applications.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q23] In Vue 3, what is the primary architectural advantage of using script setup (`<script setup>`) alongside Composition API compared to traditional Options API mixins for shared logic?
options: It automatically memoizes all reactive properties to prevent unnecessary DOM mutations.
It converts synchronous computation blocks into asynchronous Web Workers implicitly.
It allows direct manipulation of the Virtual DOM without passing through the Vue reactivity proxy system.
It eliminates namespace collision risks and maintains explicit variable provenance through direct lexical scoping.
questions.correctAnswer: It eliminates namespace collision risks and maintains explicit variable provenance through direct lexical scoping.
questions.explanation: Script setup uses true lexical scoping. When multiple mixins in the Options API contributed properties to the same component, property name collisions and unclear origin (provenance) of data were major maintenance issues. Composition API functions (composables) explicitly return values that are destructured or bound locally.
questions.hint: Think about how properties and methods merge or conflict when multiple logic chunks are brought into a single component.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 script setup lexical scoping vs mixin collision
questions.interviewTip: Senior interviewers look for migration experience and understanding why mixins were deprecated in favor of composables.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q24] When developing a high-performance Vue 3 application, why might an engineer choose `shallowRef()` over standard `ref()` for a large immutable dataset or external class instance?
options: To bypass deep recursive reactive proxy conversion, significantly reducing initialization CPU overhead and memory consumption.
To prevent the data from being garbage collected when the component unmounts.
To force Vue to perform synchronous DOM updates instead of batched asynchronous ticks.
To ensure that mutations to nested object properties automatically trigger watcher callbacks without requiring deep: true.
questions.correctAnswer: To bypass deep recursive reactive proxy conversion, significantly reducing initialization CPU overhead and memory consumption.
questions.explanation: shallowRef() tracks reactivity only on the .value access itself, rather than recursively converting all nested properties into reactive proxies. For huge third-party data structures or read-heavy datasets, this avoids massive performance penalties.
questions.hint: Consider the cost of traversing and wrapping large object graphs into Proxies.
questions.relatedConcept: shallowRef performance optimization and proxy overhead
questions.interviewTip: Crucial question for frontend performance optimization at scale.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q25] In Vue 3 with Composition API, what is the core reactivity hazard when directly destructuring properties from the object returned by `reactive()`?
options: Destructuring a reactive object automatically wraps all extracted primitives into computed properties under the hood.
The destructured variable loses reactivity connection, remaining a static primitive copy of its initial value.
It triggers a runtime TypeError because reactive objects prohibit property extraction without `toRef`.
Reactivity is fully preserved, but mutations made to the destructured variable bypass Vue's virtual DOM diffing queue.
questions.correctAnswer: The destructured variable loses reactivity connection, remaining a static primitive copy of its initial value.
questions.explanation: When you destructure a reactive object created by `reactive()`, you extract ordinary JavaScript values (like numbers or strings) which do not retain the reactive getters/setters. To preserve reactivity during destructuring, `toRefs()` or `toRef()` must be used.
questions.hint: Think about what JavaScript destructuring actually does to primitive values versus object references.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Reactive Destructuring Pitfalls
questions.interviewTip: Intermediary to advanced interviewers use this to verify whether candidates truly understand JavaScript value passing versus Vue's proxy-based reactivity mechanics.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q26] What is the primary rendering and memory optimization behavior of Vue's `v-memo` directive when applied to a large list or template block?
options: It completely destroys and re-creates DOM nodes every time any dependency updates to prevent memory leaks in large arrays.
It converts the template block into a static string during compilation, entirely disabling runtime reactivity for that element.
It caches the template sub-tree and skips both virtual DOM diffing and re-rendering unless one of the dependencies in the memo array changes.
It defers the rendering of the sub-tree until the browser main thread is idle using requestIdleCallback.
questions.correctAnswer: It caches the template sub-tree and skips both virtual DOM diffing and re-rendering unless one of the dependencies in the memo array changes.
questions.explanation: `v-memo` instructs Vue to memoize a sub-tree of the template. If the values provided in the dependency array remain identical on re-render, the entire sub-tree update is skipped, significantly speeding up rendering for heavy lists.
questions.hint: Consider memoization patterns in UI frameworks and what part of the rendering pipeline is bypassed.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue Performance Optimization with v-memo
questions.interviewTip: Great for assessing advanced Vue performance tuning knowledge beyond standard computed properties and lazy loading.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q27] What happens when you mutate a Vue 3 reactive proxy object directly inside a computed property getter function?
options: It successfully updates the reactive state without any warning or side effects.
Vue automatically intercepts the write and caches the value without triggering reactivity.
It throws a static compilation error during build time.
It triggers an infinite update loop and side-effect warnings or runtime errors.
questions.correctAnswer: It triggers an infinite update loop and side-effect warnings or runtime errors.
questions.explanation: Computed properties should be pure side-effect-free functions. Mutating state inside a computed getter triggers reactive dependencies that cause re-evaluations, leading to an infinite trigger loop that Vue detects and warns against at runtime.
questions.hint: Think about whether side effects are permitted inside computed property getters.
questions.relatedConcept: computed property side effects and infinite loops
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of Vue's reactivity system rules and functional purity in computed properties.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q28] In Vue 3, what occurs when a custom directive's `mounted` hook modifies a reactive state property that is also bound via `v-model` on the host element?
questions.codeSnippet:
<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue';
const val = ref('initial');
const vCustom = {
  mounted(el) {
    val.value = 'modified';
  }
};
</script>
<template>
  <input v-model="val" v-custom />
</template>
options: The state updates, which then propagates down to update the input's value via the reactivity system during the subsequent tick.
The directive execution is ignored because directives cannot modify setup state variables.
It causes an immediate unhandled exception due to direct mutation inside a lifecycle hook.
The input element is destroyed and recreated to prevent synchronization mismatches.
questions.correctAnswer: The state updates, which then propagates down to update the input's value via the reactivity system during the subsequent tick.
questions.explanation: Custom directives have full access to scope and reactive properties via bindings or closure. Mutating a reactive ref inside `mounted` behaves normally, scheduling a DOM update to sync the bound input element via the standard reactivity pipeline.
questions.hint: Directives run during component lifecycle phases and can interact with local closure variables.
questions.relatedConcept: custom directive lifecycle hooks and state mutation
questions.interviewTip: This tests advanced comprehension of how custom directives integrate with Vue's composition API scope and reactivity updates.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q29] In Vue 3, when using `v-memo` on a large `v-for` list, what is the primary structural trade-off regarding memory and rendering complexity?
options: It entirely eliminates the component instance lifecycle hooks for hidden items to reduce memory footprints, increasing initialization latency on toggle.
It caches the VNode tree to bypass virtual DOM diffing for that item, trading additional memory for cache arrays and optimized rendering throughput.
It forces synchronous DOM reflows across the entire list whenever any single tracked property mutates, prioritizing visual consistency over frame rate.
It disables reactivity tracking globally for the specified template scope, removing the memory overhead of dependency maps at the cost of manual patch triggers.
questions.correctAnswer: It caches the VNode tree to bypass virtual DOM diffing for that item, trading additional memory for cache arrays and optimized rendering throughput.
questions.explanation: v-memo caches the sub-tree's VNode representation based on an array of dependencies. While it speeds up diffing by skipping unchanged nodes, it incurs a minor memory cost to store the cached dependency arrays and previous values.
questions.hint: Think about what Vue compares between renders to determine whether to skip a sub-tree's diffing pass.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 v-memo performance optimization and VNode caching trade-offs
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates understand the inner workings of Vue 3's compiler-informed optimizations rather than just applying directives blindly.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q30] What is the primary architectural advantage of using Vue 3's shallowRef over a standard ref when managing large, deeply nested third-party data models?
questions.codeSnippet: const largeModel = shallowRef(heavyObjectGraph);
options: It makes the object completely immutable and read-only, preventing any accidental mutations from propagating to dependent computed properties.
It moves the state object entirely out of the JavaScript heap into WebAssembly memory to bypass garbage collection pauses.
It tracks reactivity only at the root `.value` assignment level, preventing the recursive Proxy wrapping overhead on thousands of internal nested properties.
It automatically memoizes all downstream getter functions to prevent redundant calculations during heavy re-renders.
questions.correctAnswer: It tracks reactivity only at the root `.value` assignment level, preventing the recursive Proxy wrapping overhead on thousands of internal nested properties.
questions.explanation: shallowRef bypasses the deep recursive traversal that turns nested objects and arrays into reactive Proxies, significantly reducing initialization time and memory consumption for large datasets where deep reactivity is unnecessary.
questions.hint: Consider how deep reactivity is achieved using JavaScript Proxies and the performance cost on large object graphs.
questions.relatedConcept: shallowRef performance implications and memory trade-offs in Vue 3
questions.interviewTip: Often asked when discussing performance bottlenecks in dashboards or complex data visualization apps dealing with huge state trees.

title: Next.js - Test 1: Core Fundamentals & Patterns
description: Comprehensive technical evaluation for Next.js covering runtime mechanics, design principles, and problem solving.

questions.question: [Next.js • Test 1 • Q1] In Next.js App Router, what happens when a Server Component imports and attempts to execute a module that contains browser-only APIs like 'window.localStorage' during Server-Side Rendering (SSR)?
options: Next.js automatically polyfills 'window' and 'localStorage' on the server using global storage bindings.
The server execution throws a ReferenceError ('localStorage is not defined') because browser globals are absent in Node.js/Edge runtime.
Next.js silently evaluates the Server Component on the client side instead, falling back to dynamic SSR.
TypeScript compiler compilation fails during build time prior to execution.
questions.correctAnswer: The server execution throws a ReferenceError ('localStorage is not defined') because browser globals are absent in Node.js/Edge runtime.
questions.explanation: Server Components execute in a Node.js or Edge environment where browser-specific globals like 'window', 'document', and 'localStorage' do not exist. Accessing them directly causes a runtime ReferenceError unless guarded by a typeof window !== 'undefined' check or executed inside a Client Component ('use client').
questions.hint: Think about the execution environment of React Server Components versus standard client-side bundles.
questions.relatedConcept: Next.js App Router Server Component environment restrictions and browser globals
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers frequently test this to see if candidates understand the architectural boundary between Server and Client Components.

questions.question: [Next.js • Test 1 • Q2] How does Next.js handle data mutation and cache invalidation when invoking a Server Action inside a Client Component that modifies data fetched via 'fetch' with standard caching in the App Router?
options: It automatically clears the entire client-side browser memory cache and forces a full hard reload of the single-page application.
It updates the React state optimistically but requires an explicit window.location.reload() to fetch fresh server data.
It purges the Data Cache for the specified path on the server and schedules an asynchronous refresh of the Server Component payload on the client without a full page reload.
It disables all subsequent Server Actions until the next deployment cycle clears the edge cache.
questions.correctAnswer: It purges the Data Cache for the specified path on the server and schedules an asynchronous refresh of the Server Component payload on the client without a full page reload.
questions.explanation: Calling 'revalidatePath' within a Server Action invalidates the cached data associated with that route on the server. Next.js then coordinates with the client router to fetch the updated Server Component payload and merge it into the current React tree without discarding client-side state or performing a full browser reload.
questions.hint: Consider how Server Actions integrate with the Next.js Data Cache and router cache refresh mechanisms.
questions.relatedConcept: Next.js App Router Server Actions cache revalidation lifecycle
questions.interviewTip: Crucial for assessing production Next.js proficiency regarding performance optimization and data consistency.

questions.question: [Next.js • Test 1 • Q3] What happens when you use React Context directly inside a Next.js App Router Server Component without any client boundary wrapping?
options: The server evaluates the context using default values defined in createContext, ignoring any Provider component higher up in the tree.
Next.js automatically converts the Server Component into a Client Component during compilation.
The context value is fetched successfully if the provider is placed inside the root layout.tsx file.
A build or runtime error occurs because useContext and context providers rely on client-side state hooks that are unavailable during Server Component rendering.
questions.correctAnswer: A build or runtime error occurs because useContext and context providers rely on client-side state hooks that are unavailable during Server Component rendering.
questions.explanation: React Context providers and hooks like useContext rely on client-side React state execution. Server Components execute on the server and cannot consume context or be wrapped by context providers unless explicitly designated with 'use client'.
questions.hint: Consider where Server Components execute and what hooks require.
questions.relatedConcept: Next.js App Router Server Components and React Context boundaries
questions.interviewTip: Intervers ask this to verify whether candidates understand the architectural boundary between React Server Components and client-side context models.

questions.question: [Next.js • Test 1 • Q4] When utilizing Next.js `generateStaticParams` with dynamic segments in a multilingual or multi-tenant App Router setup, what is the precise impact of returning an empty array `[]` from the function?
options: No paths are statically generated at build time; all routes are determined at runtime via dynamic SSR or on-demand Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR).
The dynamic route falls back to returning a 404 Not Found error for all incoming requests.
Next.js automatically fetches all available dynamic paths from the filesystem during the first incoming request.
The build process fails with a missing static generation configuration error.
questions.correctAnswer: No paths are statically generated at build time; all routes are determined at runtime via dynamic SSR or on-demand Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR).
questions.explanation: Returning an empty array from generateStaticParams means that no pages are statically generated at build time. Depending on the page's dynamic configuration (e.g., dynamicParams = true), Next.js will render the page on-demand when first requested.
questions.hint: Think about whether an empty array means 'none built ahead of time' versus 'build failure'.
questions.relatedConcept: Next.js generateStaticParams and dynamic segment fallback behavior
questions.interviewTip: This question tests deep knowledge of static export versus hybrid rendering behavior under the App Router.

questions.question: [Next.js • Test 1 • Q5] In Next.js App Router, how does the behavior of Server Actions passed down as props to Client Components differ from passing normal server-side callback functions?
options: Server Actions are executed on the client side using WebAssembly to mimic server behavior, while normal functions execute on the server via RPC.
Server Actions automatically serialize into secure POST endpoint references, whereas normal functions cannot be passed across the Server/Client boundary and will throw a runtime serialization error.
There is no functional difference; Next.js automatically transforms any async function passed from a Server to a Client Component into an RPC endpoint.
Server Actions passed as props are automatically debounced to prevent multiple network requests, whereas normal functions execute immediately.
questions.correctAnswer: Server Actions automatically serialize into secure POST endpoint references, whereas normal functions cannot be passed across the Server/Client boundary and will throw a runtime serialization error.
questions.explanation: Next.js Server Actions explicitly require the 'use server' directive. When passed to Client Components, Next.js transforms them into unique cryptographic action IDs pointing to automatically generated POST endpoints. Normal JavaScript functions cannot be serialized across the network boundary and fail.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to closures and function references across the network boundary in React Server Components.
questions.relatedConcept: Next.js App Router Server Actions boundary serialization
questions.interviewTip: Intervers ask this to verify if the candidate understands the security and architectural constraints of passing closures and functions from Server to Client components.

questions.question: [Next.js • Test 1 • Q6] What is the primary architectural reason Next.js enforces that `generateStaticParams` runs at build time during SSG, and what happens if a requested dynamic route parameter is missing from the returned array when `dynamicParams` is set to `false`?
options: Next.js automatically falls back to client-side rendering (CSR) and fetches the missing page data via a dynamic JSON endpoint.
Next.js compiles the missing route on-the-fly and caches it globally on the CDN edge node.
Next.js returns a 404 error because static export routes must be exhaustively pre-rendered when dynamicParams is false, preventing on-demand server rendering.
