Predefined roles apply exclusively to service accounts, whereas custom roles apply only to human user identities.
questions.correctAnswer: Predefined roles are automatically updated by Google when new permissions are added to services, whereas custom roles do not receive automatic updates and must be modified manually.
questions.explanation: Google manages predefined roles and updates them automatically when new features or permissions are introduced. Custom roles, defined by users, are static snapshots of permissions at creation time and do not auto-update when GCP adds new API methods.
questions.hint: Think about maintenance overhead and lifecycle management when new service features roll out.
questions.relatedConcept: GCP IAM Predefined vs Custom Roles
questions.interviewTip: This question assesses deep administrative knowledge regarding long-term maintenance and security posture in Google Cloud Identity and Access Management.

questions.question: [GCP • Test 1 • Q27] When configuring a Google Cloud Dataflow streaming pipeline using the DirectRunner versus the DataflowRunner, which specific failure mode typically surfaces only on the distributed DataflowRunner due to worker lifecycle management?
options: Immediate OutOfMemoryError thrown on the local JVM during the first window trigger evaluation
Deterministic deadlock inside the sliding window pane aggregation logic due to single-threaded thread pooling
Silent truncation of unbounded PCollection records when watermark advancement stalls on local disk
Non-serializable user-defined DoFn closures causing worker startup crashes during pipeline initialization
questions.correctAnswer: Non-serializable user-defined DoFn closures causing worker startup crashes during pipeline initialization
questions.explanation: The DirectRunner executes pipelines locally within a single JVM, where closures and objects often implicitly inherit serialization state or run in memory. When deployed to the distributed DataflowRunner, workers serialize DoFn instances and user functions using Java serialization (or Beam coder equivalents) to send them to remote nodes, exposing non-serializable fields or classes that cause worker startup failures.
questions.hint: Think about how code and state are transported across network boundaries to remote worker nodes in distributed execution engines.
questions.relatedConcept: Apache Beam serialization and Dataflow worker lifecycle
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your practical, production-level debugging experience with Apache Beam and GCP Dataflow beyond toy local examples.

questions.question: [GCP • Test 1 • Q28] In Google Cloud IAM, what is the precise security implication of binding a primitive role (Owner, Editor, Viewer) at a project level versus a resource-level custom IAM role?
options: Primitive roles grant broad access across all current and future GCP services and include billing/permission management privileges that custom roles lack at granular scopes
Primitive roles automatically bypass VPC Service Controls perimeters, whereas custom roles are strictly bound to perimeter ingress/egress rules
Primitive roles are evaluated via eventually consistent global caches, while custom roles support synchronous read-after-write permission propagation
Primitive roles restrict service account impersonation chains to two hops, whereas custom roles permit arbitrary delegation depths
questions.correctAnswer: Primitive roles grant broad access across all current and future GCP services and include billing/permission management privileges that custom roles lack at granular scopes
questions.explanation: Primitive roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) apply project-wide and implicitly grant permissions to newly introduced GCP services and features automatically. Furthermore, the Owner and Editor roles include dangerous permissions regarding billing, project deletion, and IAM policy management which are purposefully excluded from granular predefined or custom roles.
questions.hint: Consider the scope and privilege level associated with legacy project-level access compared to fine-grained modern access control.
questions.relatedConcept: GCP IAM primitive vs predefined and custom roles
questions.interviewTip: This tests your understanding of GCP security best practices and the principle of least privilege regarding IAM design.

questions.question: [GCP • Test 1 • Q29] When configuring a Google Cloud Dataflow streaming pipeline with windowing and triggers, how does enabling speculative execution (or late data handling via allowed lateness) impact downstream state storage and watermark progression?
options: It indefinitely delays watermark progression until all out-of-order elements are observed, requiring manual watermark updates.
It retains materialized pane state in persistent storage beyond the window's close to handle late-arriving data, increasing state storage overhead until the allowed lateness horizon expires.
It forces the pipeline runner to switch from an append-only shuffle to an in-memory broadcast join, reducing overall worker CPU utilization.
It automatically drops all late records without emitting dead-letter notifications to prevent state table growth.
questions.correctAnswer: It retains materialized pane state in persistent storage beyond the window's close to handle late-arriving data, increasing state storage overhead until the allowed lateness horizon expires.
questions.explanation: Configuring allowed lateness instructs the Dataflow runner to retain the state associated with a window after the initial watermark passes the window boundary. This allows subsequent late-arriving elements to trigger updated panes, but directly increases the state storage footprint until the expiration horizon is reached.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to window state after the watermark initially closes a window when you expect late data.
questions.relatedConcept: GCP Dataflow Streaming State and Allowed Lateness Mechanics
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves stateful streaming primitives with operational cost trade-offs in serverless big data engines.

questions.question: [GCP • Test 1 • Q30] In Google Cloud Bigtable, what is the underlying mechanism and performance consequence of creating a table with non-uniform row key distributions when performing sequential high-throughput writes?
options: It triggers an automatic redistribution of tablet ranges across nodes within milliseconds, completely neutralizing write latency spikes.
It forces Bigtable to bypass the commit log and write directly to memtables, reducing durability guarantees for sequential keys.
It causes tablet server hot-spotting, where a single node managing the relevant key range bottlenecks all write traffic while other nodes remain underutilized.
It converts the underlying storage format from an LSM-tree to a distributed B-Tree, decreasing read latency at the expense of write throughput.
questions.correctAnswer: It causes tablet server hot-spotting, where a single node managing the relevant key range bottlenecks all write traffic while other nodes remain underutilized.
questions.explanation: Bigtable distributes data across tablet servers based on contiguous row key ranges. If writes are concentrated on a narrow set of sequential keys (e.g., using an incrementing timestamp or un-hashed sequential ID as the prefix), a single tablet server absorbs the write load, causing a performance hot-spot.
questions.hint: Consider how Bigtable partitions data into tablets based on row keys and what happens if all traffic hits a single range.
questions.relatedConcept: Google Cloud Bigtable Tablet Splitting and Row Key Design
questions.interviewTip: A classic systems design question testing whether the candidate understands NoSQL underlying partition strategies versus relational indexes.

title: Docker - Test 1: Core Fundamentals & Patterns
description: Comprehensive technical evaluation for Docker covering runtime mechanics, design principles, and problem solving.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q1] What happens when you execute a Docker container from an image that lacks a defined CMD or ENTRYPOINT, and you do not provide any arguments on the command line?
questions.codeSnippet: docker run --rm my-empty-image
options: Docker automatically falls back to executing '/bin/sh' inside the container.
The container exits immediately with code 0 or an error, because no default executable is specified to run.
Docker launches an interactive terminal attached to the container's root directory.
The Docker daemon throws a syntax error at build time rather than run time.
questions.correctAnswer: The container exits immediately with code 0 or an error, because no default executable is specified to run.
questions.explanation: If neither an ENTRYPOINT nor a CMD instruction is present in the image configuration (or supplied at runtime), Docker has no command to execute when the container starts up, resulting in an immediate exit.
questions.hint: Think about what the container process runs when it starts if no default binary is declared.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker CMD vs ENTRYPOINT default behavior
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify if candidates understand the fundamental container lifecycle requirement of having a primary PID 1 process.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q2] When building a multi-stage Dockerfile, what is the primary purpose of referencing a previous stage using the 'FROM <stage_name> AS <new_stage>' syntax?
questions.codeSnippet:
FROM golang:alpine AS builder
...
FROM alpine:latest
COPY --from=builder /app/binary /usr/local/bin/
options: To cache the intermediate build layers across multiple independent machines without using a remote registry.
To run multiple concurrent daemon processes inside a single final container instance.
To selectively copy artifacts or compiled binaries from a build environment into a clean, minimal runtime image.
To share environment variables securely between development and production stages.
questions.correctAnswer: To selectively copy artifacts or compiled binaries from a build environment into a clean, minimal runtime image.
questions.explanation: Multi-stage builds allow developers to use heavy toolchain images for compilation in early stages and then copy only the resulting static artifacts into a lightweight final image, keeping image sizes small and secure.
questions.hint: Consider how artifact transfer works between different FROM blocks.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker multi-stage builds and artifact copying
questions.interviewTip: Crucial for assessing production best practices regarding image size reduction and security hardening.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q3] A Docker container terminates with exit code 137. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: The user manually sent a SIGKILL (kill -9) to the container's main process.
The container's main process returned the integer 137 as its exit status.
Docker could not find the specified image and aborted the run.
The container was killed by the kernel due to an out‑of‑memory (OOM) condition.
questions.correctAnswer: The container was killed by the kernel due to an out‑of‑memory (OOM) condition.
questions.explanation: Exit code 137 equals 128 + 9, meaning the process received signal 9 (SIGKILL). Docker normally reports this when the kernel OOM killer terminates the container because it exceeded its memory limit. While a manual SIGKILL also yields 137, the most common runtime scenario in Docker is an OOM kill, especially when memory limits are set.
questions.hint: Think about how Docker reports a process killed by a signal.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker container exit codes and OOM killer behavior
questions.interviewTip: Helps assess if candidates understand how resource limits affect container lifecycles and can diagnose memory‑related failures.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q4] Given the following Dockerfile, if you modify the line that installs the "curl" package, which layers will Docker rebuild on the next `docker build`?
questions.codeSnippet:
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Install system packages
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y git
RUN apt-get install -y curl

# Add application code
COPY src/ /app/
WORKDIR /app

# Install Python dependencies
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

CMD ["python", "app.py"]
options: The modified layer and all subsequent layers (COPY, WORKDIR, pip install, CMD).
Only the layer containing the modified "curl" installation command.
All layers from the first RUN command onward, because they share the same base image.
No layers are rebuilt; Docker will use the cache for every step.
questions.correctAnswer: The modified layer and all subsequent layers (COPY, WORKDIR, pip install, CMD).
questions.explanation: Docker caches each instruction as a separate layer. Changing a line invalidates the cache for that layer and every layer that follows, because later layers depend on the filesystem state produced by earlier ones. Earlier layers (the base image and the first RUN) remain cached.
questions.hint: Consider the dependency chain between Dockerfile instructions.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker build cache invalidation and layer dependency
questions.interviewTip: Reveals whether the candidate grasps Docker's layer model, which is essential for writing efficient Dockerfiles and debugging rebuilds.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q5] Which statement best describes the primary performance benefit of using a multi‑stage Dockerfile compared to a single‑stage Dockerfile?
options: It reduces container startup latency by decreasing the number of layers.
It reduces the final image size, which speeds up image distribution.
It enables parallel execution of build stages, cutting build time.
It improves cache hit rate for subsequent builds.
questions.correctAnswer: It reduces the final image size, which speeds up image distribution.
questions.explanation: Multi‑stage builds allow you to copy only the artifacts needed at runtime into the final image, discarding build‑time dependencies. This shrinks the image size, making pushes, pulls, and deployments faster. The other options describe benefits that are not directly caused by multi‑stage builds.
questions.hint: Think about what is actually removed from the final image when you use multiple stages.
questions.relatedConcept: Multi‑stage builds – trade‑off between image size and build complexity
questions.interviewTip: Helps assess whether the candidate understands how build‑time decisions affect runtime distribution costs.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q6] For a workload that performs many small random writes on a container-mounted volume, which storage driver typically provides better I/O performance and why?
options: aufs, because its multi‑layer merging algorithm speeds up random writes.
overlay2, because it stores container files directly on the host filesystem without a separate metadata store.
overlay2, because it uses a single lower read‑only layer and a copy‑on‑write upper layer, reducing metadata overhead.
Neither; both drivers have identical I/O performance as they depend on the host filesystem.
questions.correctAnswer: overlay2, because it uses a single lower read‑only layer and a copy‑on‑write upper layer, reducing metadata overhead.
questions.explanation: overlay2 stores changes in a single writable layer atop a read‑only lower layer, which minimizes the number of inodes and directory entries the driver must manage, resulting in lower metadata overhead and better random‑write performance than aufs, which maintains more complex per‑layer bookkeeping.
questions.hint: Consider how many layers the driver has to manage for each write operation.
questions.relatedConcept: Overlay2 storage driver – I/O performance vs metadata complexity
questions.interviewTip: Reveals the candidate's knowledge of Docker storage drivers and their impact on performance‑critical workloads.

questions.question:
[Docker • Test 1 • Q7] Given the Dockerfile below, which statement accurately describes the contents of the final image produced by `docker build -t myapp .`?

```Dockerfile
# Stage 1: Build the binary
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN go build -o /app/mybinary

# Stage 2: Create a minimal runtime image
FROM alpine:3.20
COPY --from=builder /app/mybinary /usr/local/bin/mybinary
ENTRYPOINT ["mybinary"]
```
Which of the following is true about the resulting image?
options: All files copied into `/src` during the first stage are also present in the final image, increasing its size.
The Go toolchain (`go` binary) is retained in the final image because it was part of the build stage.
Docker stores the intermediate `builder` stage layers inside the final image, making it larger than necessary.
Only the `mybinary` executable is present; none of the files from the `builder` stage remain in the final image.
questions.correctAnswer: Only the `mybinary` executable is present; none of the files from the `builder` stage remain in the final image.
questions.explanation: In a multi‑stage Dockerfile, only artifacts explicitly copied with `COPY --from=` are included in the final image. The intermediate build stage (including the source code and the Go toolchain) is discarded, so the final image contains only `/usr/local/bin/mybinary` and the base Alpine layers.
questions.hint: Think about what `COPY --from=` actually transfers between stages.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker multi‑stage builds – artifact selection and image size
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to gauge whether candidates understand how multi‑stage builds keep images lean and avoid shipping build‑time dependencies.

questions.question:
[Docker • Test 1 • Q8] A Docker image defines its container start command as follows:

```Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY server.js .
CMD node server.js
```
When the container is started with `docker run --rm mynode`, what happens to a `SIGTERM` sent to the container (e.g., via `docker stop`)?
options: The signal is intercepted by the default shell (`/bin/sh -c`) and is not forwarded to `node`, causing a delayed shutdown.
The `node` process receives the `SIGTERM` because the command is executed in *exec* form, allowing signal propagation.
Docker ignores `SIGTERM` for containers that use the `CMD` instruction without an explicit `ENTRYPOINT`.
The container will terminate immediately without giving `node` a chance to handle the signal.
questions.correctAnswer: The signal is intercepted by the default shell (`/bin/sh -c`) and is not forwarded to `node`, causing a delayed shutdown.
questions.explanation: Because the `CMD` is written in *shell* form (`CMD node server.js`), Docker runs it as `/bin/sh -c "node server.js"`. Signals like `SIGTERM` are received by the shell, which does not forward them to the child `node` process, so the application does not shut down gracefully. Using the exec form (`CMD ["node","server.js"]`) would correctly propagate the signal.
questions.hint: Consider whether the command runs under a shell or directly as an executable.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker signal handling – exec form vs shell form of CMD/ENTRYPOINT
questions.interviewTip: Helps assess if candidates know the subtle but critical difference between shell and exec forms for reliable container shutdowns.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q9] In a Docker image build process, what is the effect on the final stored image size if a large temporary dependency file is added in one layer and then deleted in a subsequent layer, versus not adding it in the first place?
questions.codeSnippet:
RUN apt-get install -y huge-package && apt-get clean
RUN rm -rf /usr/lib/huge-package
options: The final image size is smaller than if the file were never installed, because the deletion removes the bytes.
The final image size remains inflated by the full size of the dependency, as each layer is an immutable snapshot and the data remains in the earlier layer's diff.
The final image size is identical to the base image because Docker uses a copy-on-write filesystem that automatically deduplicates deleted inodes.
The final image size is only half the dependency size because Docker compresses the delta between the two consecutive layers using deduplication.
questions.correctAnswer: The final image size remains inflated by the full size of the dependency, as each layer is an immutable snapshot and the data remains in the earlier layer's diff.
questions.explanation: Docker images are composed of read-only layers. When a file is added in a layer, it becomes part of that immutable snapshot. Deleting the file in a subsequent layer only records a 'whiteout' entry in the new layer; the original data still exists in the previous layer's diff. Therefore, the storage on the disk (and the visible image size in registries) includes the bytes of the file that was 'deleted'. Option 3 correctly identifies this immutable layer behavior. Option 1 is a common misconception where users assume standard file system logic applies to the final binary artifact.
questions.hint: Think about how Union filesystems handle file deletions across layers.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker Image Layer Immutability and Whiteouts
questions.interviewTip: This question probes whether candidates understand the practical implications of the Union FS for image optimization, a critical skill for reducing deployment costs and pull times. Many developers only know the syntax of 'cleaning up' without understanding the storage cost.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q10] Two Docker containers, web and db, both mount the same named volume "shared_data". The web container starts a long‑running process that writes a 500 MB log file to /shared_data/log.txt, while the db container concurrently reads from the same file for analytics. Without any coordination mechanism, what is the most likely outcome for the db container’s read operation?
options: It will block until the write finishes, guaranteeing a consistent snapshot.
Docker guarantees atomic writes to shared volumes, so the file will always be fully written before being readable.
It will receive an incomplete or corrupted file because it may read bytes while the writer is still updating the file.
The db container will read an empty file because Docker caches volume contents per container.
questions.correctAnswer: It will receive an incomplete or corrupted file because it may read bytes while the writer is still updating the file.
questions.explanation: Docker volumes do not provide atomic file writes; a reader may see a partially written file, leading to corruption or incomplete data. The reader does not block, and Docker does not enforce atomicity. Option 4 is incorrect because volume contents are not cached per container.
questions.hint: Think about how file I/O behaves when two processes write/read the same file on a shared filesystem.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker volume sharing and race conditions
questions.interviewTip: Shows that candidates understand the lack of file‑system isolation when volumes are shared.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q11] By default, which filesystem layer does Docker Engine utilize on a Linux host for storing container writable layers and images, and what is a key characteristic of its performance profile?
options: AUFS; requires kernel patches and is the default on all major distributions
Btrfs; relies on copy-on-write snapshots and is always available without extra configuration
ZFS; mandatory for Docker on Linux to ensure filesystem integrity
OverlayFS; low metadata overhead and high I/O performance for containers
questions.correctAnswer: OverlayFS; low metadata overhead and high I/O performance for containers
questions.explanation: OverlayFS is the default storage driver for Docker on most modern Linux distributions because it offers superior performance and is natively supported in mainline kernels. AUFS requires non-mainline kernel modules. Btrfs and ZFS are filesystems that can *contain* OverlayFS but are not the primary storage driver interface Docker uses by default.
questions.hint: Think about the standard Linux kernel's support for stacked filesystems.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker Linux Storage Drivers
questions.interviewTip: Tests understanding of Docker's dependency on specific Linux kernel features for efficient containerization.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q12] When building a Docker image where the base OS uses 'dpkg' (Debian/Ubuntu) and a subsequent layer performs a 'wget' operation, why is it critical to place the 'wget' command in a separate RUN instruction rather than combining it with the OS setup in a single RUN command?
questions.codeSnippet:
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
RUN curl -O http://example.com/file.tar.gz
options: To allow the Docker daemon to reuse the cached layer if the OS setup hasn't changed, even if the download URL or file changes
The 'apt-get' command prevents network access in subsequent commands within the same RUN layer
Docker forbids combining package installation and network downloads in the same instruction for security reasons
The 'wget' command will fail if executed in the same instruction as 'apt-get' due to PAM restrictions
questions.correctAnswer: To allow the Docker daemon to reuse the cached layer if the OS setup hasn't changed, even if the download URL or file changes
questions.explanation: Docker layers are cached based on the instruction hash. If you combine 'apt-get install' with 'wget', any change to the URL forces a rebuild of the entire layer, including the time-consuming package installation. Separating them allows Docker to reuse the cached package installation layer while only re-running the download if that specific instruction changes.
questions.hint: Consider how Docker's cache invalidation works when a layer's source changes.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker Layer Caching Strategy
questions.interviewTip: Tests knowledge of optimization techniques in Dockerfile authoring to reduce build times.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q13] You are creating a production Docker image for a Go web service. Which Dockerfile approach most effectively minimizes the final image size while still allowing the Go binary to be compiled?
questions.codeSnippet:
FROM golang:1.21 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN go build -o server .

FROM scratch
COPY --from=builder /app/server /server
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]
options: Install the compiler and all build dependencies in the same image, compile, then uninstall them with `apt-get purge`.
Use a multi‑stage build: compile in a golang image, then copy the binary into a minimal `scratch` (or `alpine`) image.
Compile the binary directly inside an Alpine image and keep that Alpine image as the runtime container.
Compile in a single stage but set `GOFLAGS="-ldflags '-s -w'"` to strip symbols, keeping the same base image.
questions.correctAnswer: Use a multi‑stage build: compile in a golang image, then copy the binary into a minimal `scratch` (or `alpine`) image.
questions.explanation: A multi‑stage build separates the heavyweight build environment from the final runtime image, allowing the use of a tiny `scratch` (or `alpine`) base and resulting in a dramatically smaller image. The other options still leave build‑time packages or a larger base image in the final artifact.
questions.hint: Think about separating build and runtime environments.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker multi‑stage builds for image size optimization
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to gauge whether candidates understand how Docker layers and build stages affect image bloat and security.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q14] You need to run a web application container and a side‑car log‑collector container on the same host, each limited to specific CPU cores. Which Docker run flag gives the most precise control over which cores a container can use?
options: --cpu-shares (relative weight)
--cpus (fractional CPU limit)
--cpuset-cpus (explicit list of CPU cores)
--cpu-quota/--cpu-period (micro‑second‑level quota)
questions.correctAnswer: --cpuset-cpus (explicit list of CPU cores)
questions.explanation: `--cpuset-cpus` lets you bind a container to an explicit set of CPU cores (e.g., `--cpuset-cpus="0,2"`), providing the finest‑grained placement control. The other flags limit amount of CPU time but do not pin the container to particular cores.
questions.hint: Look for the flag that lets you pick exact core numbers.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker resource constraints – CPU pinning with cpuset
questions.interviewTip: This checks whether the candidate can differentiate between relative weighting, fractional limits, and strict core affinity.

questions.question:
[Docker • Test 1 • Q15] A Dockerfile for a Python web service contains the following lines:

```
COPY . /app
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
```

A reviewer points out that this approach causes the entire application source to be cached in every build step, resulting in long rebuild times when only dependencies change. Which idiomatic Dockerfile pattern should be used to take advantage of layer caching for dependency installation?
questions.codeSnippet:
COPY requirements.txt /app/
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . /app
options: Use ADD instead of COPY.
Run pip install before copying source.
Use a .dockerignore to exclude the source directory.
Copy only requirements.txt first, run pip install, then copy the rest of the source.
questions.correctAnswer: Copy only requirements.txt first, run pip install, then copy the rest of the source.
questions.explanation: The recommended idiomatic pattern is to copy just the requirements file, install dependencies, and then copy the rest of the source. This keeps the dependency layer cache intact when the source changes.
questions.hint: Think about which part of the build can be cached if it doesn’t change often.
questions.relatedConcept: Dockerfile layer caching and multi‑stage build patterns
questions.interviewTip: Reviewers often flag inefficient Dockerfile layering that hurts CI speed.

questions.question:
[Docker • Test 1 • Q16] A Dockerfile for a Node.js application ends with:

```
RUN adduser --disabled-password appuser
USER appuser
```

A reviewer asks why not use the default root user. Which idiomatic best practice is demonstrated by this snippet?
questions.codeSnippet:
RUN adduser --disabled-password appuser
USER appuser
options: The container runs as a non‑root user, improving security.
The container will run as root, ensuring full filesystem permissions.
The adduser command creates a user with root privileges.
The USER instruction is ignored when a container is run with docker run --user.
questions.correctAnswer: The container runs as a non‑root user, improving security.
questions.explanation: Running the application as a non‑root user is an idiomatic Docker best practice that enhances container security by limiting permissions.
questions.hint: Consider the security implications of the user that the container process runs as.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker security best practices – running as non‑root
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers check that candidates understand why containers should avoid running as root.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q17] You run `docker run -d myapp:latest` and the container exits immediately. Inspecting the logs shows the line: `exec: "python3": executable file not found in $PATH`. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: The host machine's PATH variable is not forwarded into the container, hiding the binary.
The image's Dockerfile does not install Python3, so the binary is missing at runtime.
The container was started with the `--user` flag, preventing it from accessing system binaries.
Docker's default seccomp profile blocks execution of the `python3` binary.
questions.correctAnswer: The image's Dockerfile does not install Python3, so the binary is missing at runtime.
questions.explanation: The log explicitly says the executable `python3` cannot be found inside the container. This means the image does not contain the binary, i.e., the Dockerfile failed to install it (e.g., missing `apt-get install python3`). The other options describe unrelated mechanisms that would not produce this exact error message.
questions.hint: Look at what the error message is actually complaining about.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker image build – ensuring required binaries are present in the final image
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify that candidates understand the difference between host and container environments and can debug missing dependencies.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q18] When executing `docker-compose up` as a regular user, you receive the error: `Cannot connect to the Docker daemon at unix:///var/run/docker.sock. Is the docker daemon running?` Assuming the Docker service is active, what is the most common reason for this failure?
options: The `docker-compose.yml` file contains a syntax error that prevents the daemon from being reached.
Docker's rootless mode is enabled, which disables socket access for non‑root users.
The current user is not a member of the `docker` group, so they lack permission to access the Docker socket.
The `DOCKER_HOST` environment variable points to a non‑existent remote daemon.
questions.correctAnswer: The current user is not a member of the `docker` group, so they lack permission to access the Docker socket.
questions.explanation: If the Docker daemon is running but the socket cannot be accessed, the typical cause is insufficient permissions on `/var/run/docker.sock`. Adding the user to the `docker` group resolves this. The other options either would result in different error messages or are less common in this context.
questions.hint: Think about Unix file permissions for the Docker socket.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker daemon access control – user permissions for `/var/run/docker.sock`
questions.interviewTip: This checks whether candidates know how Linux permissions affect Docker CLI operations and the proper steps to grant access.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q19] In a multi-platform CI/CD pipeline, you execute `docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64,linux/amd64 -t myapp:latest .` followed by `docker run myapp:latest`. On a standard x86_64 host without QEMU binfmt_misc registered, what is the most likely immediate outcome?
questions.codeSnippet: docker run -i -t myimage < log.txt
options: Adding `-t` causes the container to allocate a pseudo-TTY, which is compatible with file redirection and ensures the exit code is captured correctly.
Adding `-t` is harmless and standard practice to ensure output buffering is flushed to the file immediately.
The exit code is always 0 regardless of TTY allocation because Docker isolates the process exit from the CLI shell.

Adding `-t` while redirecting from a non-TTY source (like a file) causes Docker to fail with 'the input device is not a TTY' or similar stdio error on many platforms, though `-i` alone is sufficient for piping.
questions.correctAnswer: Adding `-t` while redirecting from a non-TTY source (like a file) causes Docker to fail with 'the input device is not a TTY' or similar stdio error on many platforms, though `-i` alone is sufficient for piping.
questions.explanation: The `-t` flag requests a pseudo-TTY. When standard input is redirected from a file (`< log.txt`), the input is not a TTY. Requesting a TTY when the input source is not a TTY often leads to errors like 'input device is not a TTY' or weird buffering behavior because the TTY driver expects terminal characteristics. `-i` is sufficient for piping streams. The exit code is NOT always 0; Docker propagates the container's exit code to the CLI process.
questions.hint: Think about what `-t` actually allocates and whether a file handle is a terminal.
questions.relatedConcept: TTY allocation vs Stdin redirection in Docker CLI
questions.interviewTip: Tests understanding

questions.question:
[Docker • Test 1 • Q20] Consider the following Dockerfile snippet. When a container built from this image is started, what will Docker report as the container's health status after the healthcheck runs the first three times?

```Dockerfile
FROM alpine:3.18
HEALTHCHECK --interval=5s --retries=3 --timeout=2s CMD /usr/local/bin/check.sh
CMD ["sh", "-c", "while true; do sleep 3600; done"]
```
options: unhealthy
healthy
starting
no healthcheck defined
questions.correctAnswer: healthy
questions.explanation: The healthcheck is configured with three retries. The first two executions of /usr/local/bin/check.sh exit with status 1 (failure). The third execution exits with status 0 (success). A successful run resets the failure counter, so Docker marks the container as **healthy**. It would become unhealthy only after three consecutive failures.
questions.hint: A successful healthcheck clears the previous failure count.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker healthcheck behavior and retry logic
questions.interviewTip: Shows whether the candidate understands how Docker interprets healthcheck exit codes and the effect of the retries parameter.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q21] Which Docker logging driver stores container logs as JSON files on the host and allows log rotation using the `--log-opt max-size` and `--log-opt max-file` options?
options: syslog
journald
json-file
fluentd
questions.correctAnswer: json-file
questions.explanation: The **json-file** driver writes logs to `/var/lib/docker/containers/<container-id>/<container-id>-json.log` in JSON format. It natively supports rotation via the `max-size` and `max-file` log‑options. The other drivers either forward logs to external systems (syslog, fluentd) or rely on the host's journal (journald) and do not handle file rotation themselves.
questions.hint: Look for the driver that keeps logs locally as JSON.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker logging driver configuration and log rotation
questions.interviewTip: Tests knowledge of default logging behavior and practical log‑management options in production deployments.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q22] During a Docker build, which statement about the purpose and effect of a `.dockerignore` file is correct?
options: It only prevents files from being added with the `ADD` instruction, but `COPY` still includes them.
The file must be named `.dockerignore.txt` for Docker to recognize it.
Wildcard patterns are not supported; each file must be listed explicitly.
It excludes matching files and directories from the build context that is sent to the Docker daemon.
questions.correctAnswer: It excludes matching files and directories from the build context that is sent to the Docker daemon.
questions.explanation: Docker reads `.dockerignore` relative to the root of the build context and omits any matching paths before sending the context to the daemon, reducing transfer size and build time. The other options are false: the file applies to both `ADD` and `COPY`, the name must be exactly `.dockerignore`, and glob patterns are fully supported.
questions.hint: Consider what data is transferred to the Docker daemon before any Dockerfile instructions run.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker build context filtering with .dockerignore
questions.interviewTip: Shows whether the candidate understands how to optimise build size and speed, a common real‑world concern.

questions.question:
[Docker • Test 1 • Q23] Given the following Dockerfile snippet, what will Docker do when the health‑check command fails three consecutive times?

```Dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost/ || exit 1

CMD ["myapp"]
```
Assume the container is started with `--restart=always`.
questions.codeSnippet:
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost/ || exit 1

CMD ["myapp"]
options: Docker will mark the container as **unhealthy** but will not restart it.
Docker will automatically restart the container according to the `--restart=always` policy.
Docker will stop the container and remove it from the host.
Docker will ignore the failure and continue reporting the container as healthy.
questions.correctAnswer: Docker will mark the container as **unhealthy** but will not restart it.
questions.explanation: A health‑check failure only changes the container's health status to *unhealthy*; it does not cause the container to exit. Restart policies are triggered only when the main process terminates, not when the health check fails. Therefore the container stays running but is reported as unhealthy.
questions.hint: Separate the concepts of container health status and container lifecycle.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker HEALTHCHECK behavior and restart policies
questions.interviewTip: Tests understanding of runtime monitoring features and how they differ from process management.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q24] When profiling a Docker container's startup time, which architecture introduces the highest latency due to the overhead of executing a PID 1 init process and re-executing the main application binary?
options: Standard Docker container with a single ENTRYPOINT command
Docker-in-Docker (DinD) privileged sidecar
Kubernetes DaemonSet Pod with hostPath volumes
Docker Desktop with WSL2 backend on Windows
questions.correctAnswer: Docker-in-Docker (DinD) privileged sidecar
questions.explanation: Docker-in-Docker requires starting a daemon inside the container, which involves initializing a full userland (init, networking stack, filesystem) before the application can start, adding hundreds of milliseconds to seconds of latency. The other options have lower or more predictable startup overheads relative to the complexity of the nested environment.
questions.hint: Consider the necessary initialization steps for a containerized daemon inside another container.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker-in-Docker startup latency and init overhead
questions.interviewTip: Tests understanding of nested virtualization/containerization costs, a critical factor in CI/CD pipeline speed.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q25] In a high-throughput microservice deployed as a Docker container, why does increasing the `--cpus` cgroup limit from 0.5 to 4.0 often result in diminishing returns for parallelized workloads?
options: The Docker engine introduces a fixed per-connection network overhead that scales linearly with CPU cores.
The overlayfs storage driver cannot handle concurrent read I/O operations, causing bottlenecks regardless of CPU allocation.
Context switching and lock contention within the application's runtime (JVM/Go runtime) introduce overhead that cancels out additional compute resources.
Docker's default seccomp profile restricts the number of concurrent syscalls per process to a low number.
questions.correctAnswer: Context switching and lock contention within the application's runtime (JVM/Go runtime) introduce overhead that cancels out additional compute resources.
questions.explanation: While giving more CPUs allows more threads, internal contention (locks, garbage collection, context switching) often becomes the bottleneck. Network overhead is not linear with CPU cores, storage driver limits are I/O-bound not CPU-bound, and seccomp does not limit syscall concurrency rates in this manner.
questions.hint: Think about Amdahl's Law and internal synchronization costs in complex runtimes.
questions.relatedConcept: Amdahl's Law and internal contention in containerized runtimes
questions.interviewTip: Assesses if candidates understand that resource limits don't equate to linear performance gains in complex software.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q26] Given the following Dockerfile snippet, what will Docker report as the container's health status after it has been running for 2 minutes, assuming the application never starts listening on port 8080?
questions.codeSnippet:
FROM alpine:3.18
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --retries=3 CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1
options: healthy
starting
no healthcheck
unhealthy
questions.correctAnswer: unhealthy
questions.explanation: The healthcheck runs every 30 s, allowing up to 3 retries. Because the curl command always fails, after the first 3 attempts Docker marks the container as **unhealthy**. The status does not stay "starting" once the retry limit is exceeded, and a HEALTHCHECK instruction is present, so "no healthcheck" is incorrect.
questions.hint: Count the retries and consider what happens when they all fail.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker healthcheck status transitions
questions.interviewTip: Shows whether the candidate knows that healthchecks are informational only and that Docker marks the container unhealthy after the retry limit is reached.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q27] A container is started with the command `docker run --restart=on-failure:2 myapp`. If the container exits with status code 0 three times consecutively, how many restart attempts will Docker perform?
questions.explanation: The `on-failure` restart policy only triggers when the container exits with a non‑zero status. Exits with code 0 are considered successful, so Docker will not restart the container at all, regardless of the `:2` limit.
questions.hint: Consider what "failure" means for this policy.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker restart policy (on-failure) semantics
questions.interviewTip: Tests understanding of how Docker distinguishes between normal exits and failures when applying restart policies.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q28] A Dockerfile builds successfully on a developer's macOS machine using the default Docker Engine. The image is pushed to a registry and pulled on a CI runner using Linux with a different architecture. The container fails to start with 'Exec format error'. What is the primary cause of this incompatibility?
options: The Linux CI runner is using a different storage driver version than the macOS Docker Desktop.
The image was built for the host's architecture (e.g., ARM64 on Apple Silicon) and the CI runner expects a different architecture (e.g., AMD64).
The entrypoint script uses shell syntax specific to the 'sh' shell on macOS, which is not installed in the Linux base image.
The registry protocol version used during push differs from the version used during pull, causing binary corruption.
questions.correctAnswer: The image was built for the host's architecture (e.g., ARM64 on Apple Silicon) and the CI runner expects a different architecture (e.g., AMD64).
questions.explanation: Docker images are architecture-specific. If a build occurs on an ARM-based host (like recent Macs) without cross-compilation flags, the resulting binary and image tags are for ARM64. When pulled on an AMD64 Linux runner, the kernel cannot execute the ARM binaries, resulting in 'Exec format error'. Storage drivers and registry protocols are not the cause of binary execution failures.
questions.hint: Consider the CPU architecture differences between modern laptops and standard cloud CI nodes.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker Image Architecture Compatibility and Cross-Platform Builds
questions.interviewTip: Tests understanding of target architectures in CI/CD pipelines and the need for multi-arch builds.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q29] A Dockerfile includes the instruction COPY --chmod=755 app.sh /app/. This build succeeds on Docker Engine 24.0 but fails with an 'unknown flag' error on an older Docker Engine version. What feature is being tested here and why did it fail on the older version?
questions.codeSnippet:
FROM alpine
COPY --chmod=755 app.sh /app/
options: The permissions 755 are invalid for the Alpine base image, causing a filesystem-level rejection during file extraction.
The COPY instruction requires the source file to exist in the build context's root directory, and 'app.sh' was missing during the older build.
The --chmod flag is a BuildKit feature that requires explicit enablement in older versions and is not part of the original 'docker build' legacy engine.
Older Docker Engine versions do not support the 'COPY' command for executable scripts, requiring 'ADD' instead.
questions.correctAnswer: The --chmod flag is a BuildKit feature that requires explicit enablement in older versions and is not part of the original 'docker build' legacy engine.
questions.explanation: The --chmod flag for the COPY instruction was introduced with BuildKit. In older Docker Engine versions using the legacy builder, this flag is unknown and causes a build error. This highlights the difference between legacy and BuildKit build engines and their feature sets. Permissions 755 are valid, file existence is a separate error, and ADD is not required for executables.
questions.hint: Think about the evolution of Docker's build engines (Legacy vs. BuildKit) and feature availability.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker BuildKit vs. Legacy Build Engine Feature Parity
questions.interviewTip: Assesses awareness of Docker versioning, build engine differences, and portability of Dockerfiles across environments.

questions.question: [Docker • Test 1 • Q30] A microservice in a Docker Swarm cluster must serve HTTP traffic to the outside world on port 80 **and** communicate privately with another service in the same stack over a network that spans multiple nodes. Which Docker network configuration best balances external exposure, inter-service isolation, and network performance?
options: Use the default bridge network for both services.
Run both services with the host network driver.
Create a macvlan network for the HTTP service and a bridge network for the private service.
Configure both services to use an overlay network and expose the HTTP service via the Swarm ingress controller.
questions.correctAnswer: Configure both services to use an overlay network and expose the HTTP service via the Swarm ingress controller.
questions.explanation: Overlay networks with the Swarm ingress controller provide automatic load balancing, service discovery, and isolation across multiple nodes while still allowing external access to the HTTP service. The bridge driver is limited to a single host and would not work across nodes; the host driver removes network isolation entirely; and a macvlan network adds unnecessary complexity and does not integrate with Swarm’s built‑in routing mesh.
questions.hint: Consider how Docker Swarm routes external requests to services and how inter‑node networking works.
questions.relatedConcept: Docker Swarm networking and overlay networks
questions.interviewTip: This question probes a senior engineer’s awareness of deployment topology, security isolation, and performance trade‑offs when scaling services across a cluster.

title: Kubernetes - Test 1: Core Fundamentals & Patterns
description: Comprehensive technical evaluation for Kubernetes covering runtime mechanics, design principles, and problem solving.

questions.question: [Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q1] A Kubernetes cluster relies on the kubelet's automatic client certificate rotation (the default behavior). An administrator disables the `--rotate-certificates` flag on all nodes and then restarts the kubelet process without supplying a fresh client certificate. After the existing client certificate expires, what is the most likely result when the kubelet tries to communicate with the API server?
options: The kubelet automatically creates a new self‑signed client certificate and resumes normal communication.
The kubelet fails to authenticate, the node is marked NotReady, but the pods already running on the node continue to operate.
The kubelet falls back to using the node's bootstrap token for authentication and re‑joins the cluster.
The kubelet process terminates, and the node is evicted from the cluster after a grace period.
questions.correctAnswer: The kubelet fails to authenticate, the node is marked NotReady, but the pods already running on the node continue to operate.
questions.explanation: When `--rotate-certificates` is disabled, the kubelet will not request a new client certificate. After the current certificate expires, the kubelet cannot authenticate to the API server, causing the node controller to mark the node NotReady. Existing pods are not killed; they keep running until the node is manually fixed or removed.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when a client certificate becomes invalid and the kubelet cannot obtain a new one.
questions.relatedConcept: kubelet client certificate rotation and node health status
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify the candidate understands kubelet authentication mechanisms and the impact of disabling automatic certificate rotation on node availability.

questions.question:
[Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q2] A cluster has two mutating admission webhooks configured for pod creation:

- Webhook A: `failurePolicy: Fail`
- Webhook B: `failurePolicy: Ignore`

Both webhooks have `sideEffects: None`. During a pod creation request, Webhook A experiences a network timeout, while Webhook B succeeds and returns a mutation. What will be the final outcome of the pod creation request?
options: The pod creation proceeds with only the mutation applied by Webhook B.
The pod creation proceeds with no mutations because the failure of Webhook A aborts the entire request.
The pod creation is rejected and the API server returns an error to the client.
The API server automatically retries Webhook A until it succeeds before completing the request.
questions.correctAnswer: The pod creation is rejected and the API server returns an error to the client.
questions.explanation: A webhook with `failurePolicy: Fail` causes the entire admission request to be rejected if the webhook call fails (including a timeout). Even though Webhook B succeeded, the failure of Webhook A aborts the request, so the pod is not created.
questions.hint: Consider how the `failurePolicy` setting influences request handling when a webhook call fails.
questions.relatedConcept: Admission webhook failure policies and request flow
questions.interviewTip: This question checks whether the candidate knows the semantics of `failurePolicy` in admission webhooks and can reason about mixed‑policy configurations.

questions.question: [Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q3] A `PodDisruptionBudget` (PDB) is configured with `unavailable: 1` for a Deployment running 5 replicas. During a node drain, the kubelet observes that the current number of available replicas is already 1. What is the immediate consequence for the drain operation regarding the remaining pods on that node?
options: The drain proceeds immediately because the PDB allows up to 1 unavailable, and currently exactly 1 is unavailable.
The drain fails with an error code, rolling back the cordon status instantly without waiting.
The PDB is ignored because it only applies to voluntary evictions triggered by `kubectl delete`, not node cordons.
The drain blocks and waits for additional replicas to become Available before proceeding, effectively violating the `minAvailable` equivalent constraint.
questions.correctAnswer: The drain blocks and waits for additional replicas to become Available before proceeding, effectively violating the `minAvailable` equivalent constraint.
questions.explanation: A PDB with `unavailable: 1` ensures at most 1 pod is unavailable, meaning at least N-1 (4) must be available. If only 1 is currently available, the system is already in a state that violates the *implicit* `minAvailable=4` requirement. The eviction API will check the current availability against the PDB's allowed unavailability. Since making any additional pod unavailable would result in 2+ unavailable pods (violating `unavailable: 1`), the eviction is blocked. It does not fail immediately; it waits until the availability recovers to a state where the eviction would be permissible.
questions.hint: Think about the complement of 'unavailable' in the context of current cluster health.
questions.relatedConcept: Pod Disruption Budgets and eviction machinery interaction during node drain
questions.interviewTip: Tests understanding that PDBs are gates for evictions, not hard failures, and how 'unavailable' is evaluated against the current live state.

questions.question: [Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q4] In a Kubernetes manifest, a `Service` is defined with `sessionAffinity: ClientIP` and `sessionAffinityConfig: { clientIP: { timeoutSeconds: 10800 } }`. Which of the following statements accurately describes the behavior of the `timeoutSeconds` field?
questions.codeSnippet:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
spec:
  sessionAffinity: ClientIP
  sessionAffinityConfig:
    clientIP:
      timeoutSeconds: 10800
options: It indicates the duration for which the client-to-pod affinity mapping is remembered in the IPVS or iptables rules; if the client reconnects after this period, they may be routed to a different pod.
It defines the maximum time a client IP can maintain a sticky connection before the Service endpoint controller removes it from the affinity cache entirely.
It specifies the keep-alive duration for individual TCP connections proxied by kube-proxy, after which they are terminated regardless of the client's activity.
It is the timeout for the health check probes associated with the Service's endpoints; if a pod fails health checks for this duration, it is removed from the Service.
questions.correctAnswer: It indicates the duration for which the client-to-pod affinity mapping is remembered in the IPVS or iptables rules; if the client reconnects after this period, they may be routed to a different pod.
questions.explanation: The `sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP.timeoutSeconds` field controls how long the Kubernetes control plane (specifically the Service controller and endpoints) retains the mapping between a specific client IP and a specific pod. If the client IP does not interact with the Service for this duration, the mapping expires, and subsequent traffic from that IP may be balanced to any available pod. It does not control TCP keep-alives, health check timeouts, or the lifetime of the connection itself, but rather the statefulness of the routing table entries generated by kube-proxy.
questions.hint: This setting governs the lifetime of the routing rule, not the network connection itself.
questions.relatedConcept: Service Session Affinity configuration semantics
questions.interviewTip: Distinguishes between application-level connection timeouts and infrastructure-level routing state persistence, a common source of debugging difficulties in microservices.

questions.question: [Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q5] A MutatingAdmissionWebhook receives a pod creation request and responds with HTTP 200 and a JSON body containing a malformed JSON Patch (e.g., missing a comma). How does the Kubernetes API server respond to the original client request?
options: 400 Bad Request
500 Internal Server Error
422 Unprocessable Entity
403 Forbidden
questions.correctAnswer: 500 Internal Server Error
questions.explanation: When a mutating webhook returns a patch that cannot be parsed or applied, the API server treats this as an internal failure and rejects the request with a 500 Internal Server Error, indicating that it could not process the admission response.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when the server cannot apply the transformation supplied by the webhook.
questions.relatedConcept: Admission webhook error handling – malformed JSON Patch response
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates understand the strict contract between webhooks and the API server and how failures are surfaced to users.

questions.question: [Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q6] A user attempts to create a ConfigMap with the name "my-configuration-settings-that-exceed-the-maximum-allowed-length-of-sixty-three-characters". What HTTP status code does the Kubernetes API server return for this request?
options: 400 Bad Request
404 Not Found
422 Unprocessable Entity
409 Conflict
questions.correctAnswer: 422 Unprocessable Entity
questions.explanation: Kubernetes validates object names against the DNS-1123 subdomain format, which limits the length to 63 characters. Violations are reported as validation errors, and the API server returns 422 Unprocessable Entity to indicate the request is syntactically correct but semantically invalid.
questions.hint: The error is a validation failure, not a missing resource or a conflict.
questions.relatedConcept: API server validation – resource name length constraints
questions.interviewTip: This tests knowledge of built‑in validation rules and the semantics of the 422 status code in the Kubernetes API.

questions.question:
[Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q7] You have a manifest file `pod.yaml` that defines a Pod but also includes an unknown field `spec.unknownField: true`. What will happen when you run the two dry‑run modes of kubectl?

```bash
kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f pod.yaml
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f pod.yaml
```
options: Both commands succeed because dry‑run does not perform any schema validation.
Server‑side dry‑run succeeds, but client‑side dry‑run fails with a validation error.
Both commands fail with the same validation error.
Client‑side dry‑run succeeds, but server‑side dry‑run fails with a validation error.
questions.correctAnswer: Client‑side dry‑run succeeds, but server‑side dry‑run fails with a validation error.
questions.explanation: Client‑side dry‑run only validates the manifest against the local kubectl schema, which ignores unknown fields, so it succeeds. Server‑side dry‑run sends the object to the API server where the OpenAPI validation rejects the unknown field, returning a BadRequest error. Therefore only the server‑side mode fails.
questions.hint: Consider where the actual schema validation occurs in each dry‑run mode.
questions.relatedConcept: Difference between client‑side and server‑side dry‑run validation in kubectl
questions.interviewTip: Shows whether the candidate knows that server‑side dry‑run performs full admission validation while client‑side only checks basic syntax.

questions.question:
[Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q8] Using the Go client‑go dynamic client, a developer writes the following code to delete a namespaced resource:

```go
res := dynamicClient.Resource(schema.GroupVersionResource{Group: "apps", Version: "v1", Resource: "deployments"}).Namespace("prod")
err := res.Delete(context.TODO(), "", metav1.DeleteOptions{})
```
What error response does the Kubernetes API server return?
options: A BadRequest error with the message "name must be provided".
A NotFound error because an empty name matches no object.
A Forbidden error because empty names are prohibited for security reasons.
The request succeeds and deletes all Deployments in the "prod" namespace.
questions.correctAnswer: A BadRequest error with the message "name must be provided".
questions.explanation: The Delete subresource requires a non‑empty name. The API server validates the request and returns a 400 BadRequest with a message indicating that the name field is required. It does not interpret an empty string as a wildcard, nor does it treat it as a NotFound or Forbidden case.
questions.hint: Think about the required fields for a DELETE request on a specific resource.
questions.relatedConcept: Kubernetes API validation of required fields in DELETE requests using client-go
questions.interviewTip: Tests understanding of how the API server enforces request payload constraints, not just client‑side errors.

questions.question: [Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q9] Kubernetes API server implements request priority and fairness (flow control). If a client request is submitted to a priority level whose `maxRequestsInFlight` quota is already fully utilized, what does the apiserver do with that request?
options: It is immediately rejected with an HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) response.
It is placed in the priority level's waiting queue and will be processed once a running slot frees up.
The request is automatically downgraded to a lower priority level.
The apiserver silently drops the request without sending any response.
questions.correctAnswer: It is placed in the priority level's waiting queue and will be processed once a running slot frees up.
questions.explanation: When `maxRequestsInFlight` for a priority level is reached, the apiserver does not reject the request outright; instead it enqueues the request in that priority level's waiting queue. The request will be dequeued and processed as soon as a running slot becomes available, preserving fairness across clients. The other options describe behaviours that are not part of the flow‑control design.
questions.hint: Think about how the apiserver avoids rejecting clients outright while still respecting limits.
questions.relatedConcept: Kubernetes API Server request flow control and priority levels
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to gauge understanding of apiserver internals and how Kubernetes protects itself from overload.

questions.question:
[Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q10] Consider the following Job manifest:
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: backoff-job
spec:
  backoffLimit: 3
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 300
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: work
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "exit 1"]
```
If the pod created by this Job exits with a non‑zero status, how does the Job controller behave?
questions.codeSnippet:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: backoff-job
spec:
  backoffLimit: 3
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 300
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: work
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "exit 1"]
options: The Job marks itself as Failed after the first pod exit and does not create any additional pods, ignoring `backoffLimit`.
The Job treats the pod as succeeded because `restartPolicy: Never` means the container will not be restarted, so the job completes successfully.
The Job creates a new pod for each failure, up to a total of three retries, because `restartPolicy: Never` prevents pod restarts but the Job controller can still launch replacement pods.
The `activeDeadlineSeconds` causes the Job to be terminated immediately, regardless of the backoff limit.
questions.correctAnswer: The Job creates a new pod for each failure, up to a total of three retries, because `restartPolicy: Never` prevents pod restarts but the Job controller can still launch replacement pods.
questions.explanation: `restartPolicy: Never` tells the kubelet not to restart the container inside the same pod. However, the Job controller can still create new pods when a pod fails, and it will do so until the number of failed attempts reaches `backoffLimit`. Therefore the Job will retry up to three times (four pod creations total) before marking the Job as Failed. The other options misinterpret the interaction between restartPolicy, backoffLimit, and Job completion semantics.
questions.hint: Separate the concepts of container restarts inside a pod from the Job controller's ability to spawn new pods.
questions.relatedConcept: Kubernetes Job controller retry logic with `restartPolicy`, `backoffLimit`, and `activeDeadlineSeconds`
questions.interviewTip: This tests deep knowledge of batch API semantics, a common source of confusion for candidates who mix up pod‑level and controller‑level retry mechanisms.

questions.question: [Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q11] A node is manually tainted with `key=maintenance:NoExecute` (effect `NoExecute`) at 12:00. A pod on that node has a toleration for the same key and effect with `tolerationSeconds: 90`. The node becomes NotReady at 12:05 and stays NotReady. When will the pod be evicted by the kubelet?
options: 12:06:30 (90 seconds after the node became NotReady)
12:02:00 (120 seconds after the taint was added)
The pod will remain until the node is marked Ready again
12:01:30 (90 seconds after the taint was added)
questions.correctAnswer: 12:01:30 (90 seconds after the taint was added)
questions.explanation: For `NoExecute` taints, `tolerationSeconds` is measured from the moment the taint is added (`timeAdded`). After the specified seconds elapse, the kubelet evicts the pod regardless of the node's Ready condition. Therefore eviction occurs at 12:01:30, which is 90 seconds after 12:00.
questions.hint: Count 90 seconds from when the taint was applied, not from when the node became NotReady.
questions.relatedConcept: NoExecute taints and tolerationSeconds timing
questions.interviewTip: Tests deep knowledge of how taints, tolerations, and node conditions interact, a common source of subtle bugs in production clusters.

questions.question: [Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q12] In a cluster with 5,000 Pods, a Development team requests a default Kubernetes Deployment with `replicas: 1`. An SRE argues that using a StatefulSet with `replicas: 1` for this stateless service would significantly increase control plane overhead due to stable network identifiers. Why is this argument technically incorrect regarding the primary performance trade-off?
questions.codeSnippet:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: my-stateless-app
spec:
  serviceName: "my-stateless-app"
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-stateless-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-stateless-app
options: StatefulSet without an associated Headless Service does not create individual Endpoints or DNS records for the Pod, so the control plane overhead is negligible and identical to a Deployment at scale 1.
StatefulSets require manual volume provisioning for each replicated Pod, causing scheduler contention that is orders of magnitude higher than Deployment scheduling.
Deployments automatically enable horizontal scaling, which pre-allocates CIDR ranges for all potential replicas, whereas StatefulSets allocate CIDRs on-demand, making the latter more efficient.
The API server validates StatefulSet ownership via finalizers that block garbage collection of the backing PVC, creating significant I/O bottlenecks on etcd.
questions.correctAnswer: StatefulSet without an associated Headless Service does not create individual Endpoints or DNS records for the Pod, so the control plane overhead is negligible and identical to a Deployment at scale 1.
questions.explanation: A StatefulSet requires a `serviceName` to provide stable network identity (DNS) and unique IPs. If no Headless Service exists (or if the Service does not resolve the Pods, e.g., selector mismatch), the StatefulSet controller does not create DNS records or stable endpoints for the Pod. Therefore, the control plane overhead (API server watch, scheduler decisions) is similar to a Deployment. Option B is wrong because volume provisioning is only necessary for persistent storage, not inherent to the resource type. Option C is wrong because CIDR allocation is handled by CNI plugins per Pod, not pre-allocated for the Deployment spec. Option D is wrong because PVC finalizers only apply if volumes are actually claimed and specified in the volumeClaimTemplates.
questions.hint: Consider what components (DNS, Endpoints, Volumes) are actually created when a StatefulSet is applied without specific storage requirements or a service.
questions.relatedConcept: StatefulSet vs Deployment resource overhead and network identity requirements
questions.interviewTip: Tests if the candidate understands that 'Stateful' implies storage and network guarantees, but these are only incurred when the corresponding services/volumes are configured, rather than assuming the resource type itself imposes a fixed penalty.

questions.question: [Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q13] A node is experiencing memory pressure and the kubelet initiates eviction. Which pods will it evict first according to the default eviction algorithm?
options: Pods that have the highest memory requests are evicted first.
Pods with the lowest priority class (or lowest QoS if no priority class is set) are evicted first.
Pods that are currently terminating are evicted before running pods.
Pods with the highest CPU limits are evicted first.
questions.correctAnswer: Pods with the lowest priority class (or lowest QoS if no priority class is set) are evicted first.
questions.explanation: Kubelet eviction prioritizes pods with the lowest priority class, then by QoS class, and finally by memory usage. Thus pods with the lowest priority class are removed first. The other options do not reflect the eviction order.
questions.hint: Think about priority classes and QoS before other metrics.
questions.relatedConcept: Node memory pressure and pod eviction priority
questions.interviewTip: Shows whether the candidate understands how Kubernetes protects higher‑priority workloads during resource contention.

questions.question: [Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q14] When a container's memory usage exceeds its specified limit, what is the kubelet's default response before the pod’s restart policy takes effect?
options: The runtime silently throttles the process so it never uses more than the limit.
The kubelet evicts the entire pod from the node.
The kubelet marks the pod as OOMKilled and terminates the offending process.
The pod continues running with no indication of the violation.
questions.correctAnswer: The kubelet marks the pod as OOMKilled and terminates the offending process.
questions.explanation: Exceeding a memory limit triggers the container runtime’s OOM killer, which kills the process. Kubelet then reports the pod status as OOMKilled. The pod is not automatically throttled or evicted unless the restartPolicy dictates a restart.
questions.hint: Consider what happens inside the container runtime.
questions.relatedConcept: Container memory limits and OOM handling
questions.interviewTip: Tests knowledge of how Kubernetes enforces memory limits at runtime and how pod status reflects OOM events.

questions.question: [Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q15] A Deployment named `web` creates pods that repeatedly enter the `CrashLoopBackOff` state. The pod's logs end with the line `Killed` and `kubectl describe pod web-xxxxx` shows the termination reason `OOMKilled`. Which action will most directly resolve the crash loop?
options: Scale the Deployment down to a single replica to reduce load.
Add a `livenessProbe` so the container is restarted earlier.
Change the image pull policy to `IfNotPresent`.
Increase the container's memory request and limit so the process has enough RAM.
questions.correctAnswer: Increase the container's memory request and limit so the process has enough RAM.
questions.explanation: The `OOMKilled` termination reason means the container exceeded its memory limit and was killed by the kernel. Raising the memory request/limit gives the process the required RAM and prevents the OOM kill, which stops the CrashLoopBackOff. Scaling replicas, adding a liveness probe, or altering the image pull policy do not address the memory shortage.
questions.hint: Check the termination reason shown by `kubectl describe`.
questions.relatedConcept: Memory limit enforcement and OOMKilled causing CrashLoopBackOff
questions.interviewTip: Shows the candidate can map a pod's termination reason to the correct resource‑configuration fix.

questions.question: [Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q16] When a Kubernetes Server-Side Apply (SSA) operation is performed on a resource without specifying a 'fieldManager', what does the API server do regarding the ownership of existing fields that conflict with the new state?
options: It applies the new configuration while preserving existing field ownership by other managers, but assumes the identity 'unknown' for the new fields.
It fails the request with a 409 Conflict error because ownership cannot be determined.
It automatically assigns the 'fieldManager' to 'kubectl' and forces ownership of all fields to that manager.
It strips the managedFields metadata from the object and treats the object as an unmanaged, last-write-wins resource.
questions.correctAnswer: It applies the new configuration while preserving existing field ownership by other managers, but assumes the identity 'unknown' for the new fields.
questions.explanation: In Kubernetes, if 'fieldManager' is omitted during a Server-Side Apply, the API server defaults the manager to 'unknown'. It does not fail; instead, it performs the apply operation. Fields already managed by other specific managers (like 'kubectl' or a specific controller) retain their ownership. The new or changed fields sent in the request are attributed to the 'unknown' manager. This behavior prevents the default failure that would occur in a standard 'update' without conflict detection, but it breaks the determinism of ownership tracking, which is why it is discouraged in production automation.
questions.hint: Consider how the API server handles anonymous or unattributed writers in the SSA tracking mechanism.
questions.relatedConcept: Kubernetes Server-Side Apply (SSA) default fieldManager behavior and ownership conflict resolution.
questions.interviewTip: This distinguishes candidates who understand the low-level mechanics of SSA from those who only know the high-level 'kubectl apply' command. It tests awareness of the 'unknown' manager edge case.

questions.question: [Kubernetes • Test 1 • Q17] You are setting up a new Kubernetes cluster using a managed service provider (e.g., EKS, GKE, AKS) with private subnets. The Cloud Provider Interface (CPI) is configured to use the 'ipMasq' feature for load balancer translation. What specific behavior does 'ipMasq' enforce on the pod-to-service traffic between nodes, and why might this be problematic for high-throughput data plane applications?
options: It disables NAT on the node, forcing pods to use direct IP routing, which fails if cross-node routing is not enabled in the CNI.

It rewrites the source IP of packets entering a node so they appear to come from the node IP, modifying the connection state in the kernel's connection tracking table and causing issues with L7 proxy statefulness.
It encrypts the payload of the traffic to ensure privacy between pods on different nodes, adding latency due to CPU encryption overhead.
It translates the service IP to the pod IP at the ingress of the cluster only, leaving inter-node traffic untouched.
questions.correctAnswer: It rewrites the source IP of packets entering a node so they appear to come from the node IP, modifying the connection state in the kernel's connection tracking table and causing issues with L7 proxy statefulness.
questions.explanation: The 'ipMasq' feature in Kubernetes Cloud Provider Interfaces (common in AWS/Azure/GCP) performs NodePort masquerading. When a pod on Node A communicates with a Service on Node B, the source IP in the packet is rewritten from the Pod IP to the Node IP (or a specific masquerade range). This changes the five-tuple seen by the service. While this simplifies firewall rules, it breaks direct connection state because the return traffic must go through the same masquerade node if stateful L7 proxies are involved. Furthermore, it prevents source IP preservation, which is critical for audit logging and certain multi-tenant security隔离 models in high-throughput scenarios. The key distinction is the modification of the source IP in the packet header, not just NAT for outbound internet traffic.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the source IP address of a packet when it crosses a node boundary to reach a Service on a different node in a masquerading configuration.
